We give the theory (a w_i proportional to 1/t_i weight split for three concurrent realizations; a het-job specification as an admissible directive) and report real results, including what the run exposed: the 1/t split assumes time linear in rows, and this fails for the MI100 rank (6 rows took 597 ms against a linear prediction of 1.6 ms). A launch-geometry model, with predictions recorded before measuring, succeeds for the A100 (time flat from 128 to 3456 rows, stepping at exactly 3520 and 6976) and places the MI100 floor in the key loop; changing its launch settings cut about 600 ms to 14.6 ms and the energy per call at 6 rows by 32x, though the MI100 remains about 95x slower than an A100 at 8192 rows. Controlled reruns show that the companion paper's 8.1x A100 result and 22 ms Gatherv were artifacts of four ranks sharing one GPU under Open MPI's default transport. A key/value-split partition whose message sizes are derived from shapes alone is then run: the ring Allreduce of the 8.5 MB message took 11.3, 16.0 and 15.3 ms against a predicted 11-12 ms, the small Allreduce missed its prediction in every run, and compute times reproduce to about 1% while communication times vary up to 4x between runs. Each idea is introduced with a figure and closed with worked examples.

items.title: Veil-Then-Reveal: Protecting PII Privacy via Reversible Pseudo-Anonymization in Zero-Trust User--LLM Interaction
items.author: Mohamed Shaaban, Mohamed Elmahallawy, Thomas E. Carroll
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly process sensitive documents and personal information, yet sending prompts containing personally identifiable information (PII) to remote providers exposes data subjects and organizations to risks from logging, retention, model training, and unintended disclosure. Existing anonymization methods often mask or remove PII, while conventional encryption eliminates the lexical and structural cues needed for effective LLM processing. We present Veil-then-Reveal (VtR), a user-side PII pseudo-anonymization framework for privacy-preserving LLM interaction under a zero-trust threat model. VtR treats remote LLM providers as untrusted and sends only pseudo-anonymized prompts, keeping plaintext PII on the user. VtR first detects PII and replaces it with realistic, same-type, in-vocabulary surrogates before prompts leave the user's device, preserving their linguistic and structural properties. It combines format-preserving encryption (FPE) for structured PII, such as phone and credit-card numbers, with a keyed-hash dictionary and secure vault for semantic PII, such as names, locations, and organizations. Session-specific mappings provide cross-session unlinkability, while user-side restoration reversibly replaces surrogates with their original values in LLM responses. We further introduce a rank-class FPE strategy for dates that preserves format and ambiguity while reducing cipher evaluations. Evaluation on three datasets containing 11,322 annotated PII instances achieves 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, and 99.9% round trip; 100% of echoed surrogates end-to-end round-trip restoration.

items.title: GRAD: Graph-Structured Antibody Defense for LLM Agents
items.author: Tianqi Song, Jiawei Du, Xuemei Jia, Zheng Wang
items.content: Memory poisoning and decomposition attacks distribute malicious evidence across the operations of large language model agents. Existing request-level defenses can miss such attacks because they assess individual inputs without connecting earlier information to later actions. Moreover, detectors must adapt as task contexts change, while updates to shared parameters can impair previously learned detection capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose GRAD, which combines graph-based evidence aggregation across operations with an extensible collection of detection experts. Its Semantic-Structural Understanding Module (SSUM) jointly encodes operation text, event attributes, and typed candidate relations in an execution graph to aggregate distributed attack evidence into a graph-level risk score. Its Continual Antibody Adaptation (CAA) adds experts on frozen encoder snapshots and routes inputs by observable graph signatures, acquiring and reusing detection capabilities as tasks arrive. Across Decomp, MCP, and MRT, GRAD achieves AUROCs of 97.19%, 77.59%, and 86.60%, respectively, outperforming Sequential Monitor and locally adapted Agent-Sentry and NeuroTaint. CAA improves final accuracy by 13.08 percentage points over Replay on the cross-dataset task stream. The gain remains 9.05 points with equal family/base-case weights within each task. Its compact drop-in gate performs local model inference in milliseconds without monitoring API calls.

items.title: Understanding KV Residency in Production-Scale Agentic LLM Workloads
items.author: Mayank Arya, Agrim Bari, Anjaly Parayil, Yogesh Simmhan, Renee St. Amant, Victor R\"uhle, Saravan Rajmohan
items.content: Agentic large language model (LLM) applications turn one user request into a sequence of model and tool calls over a growing context. Retaining this context's key-value (KV) state in GPU memory lets later calls reuse it instead of recomputing it, but at fleet scale this needs substantial memory. We characterize four production Microsoft M365 workload traces (Deep Research, Enterprise Assistant, Coding Agent and Enterprise Chat) spanning more than 121 million model calls. In Deep Research, the application issues 89% of model calls and the median context grows from about 10K to 68K tokens by the 30th call. About 80% of context tokens are served from the prefix cache. With the public Llama-2-70B KV layout standing in for confidential models, one 99th-percentile Deep Research session exceeds the 80 GB HBM of an NVIDIA H100, and holding all live sessions at their peak needs an estimated 501.8 TB of HBM, although inference occupies only 5.6% of that retention time. Trace-driven replay shows that a one-hour idle cap cuts this ceiling by 3.6x while raising the share of calls that recompute context only from 4.07% to 4.53%. Under tighter budgets, eviction alone is insufficient: at one tenth of the busiest hour's demand, LRU eviction makes 63% of Deep Research calls recompute and clairvoyant furthest-next-use 31%, whereas multi-resolution retention (MRR), which demotes the LRU session's KV state to int4, lowers this to 13.6%. Placement imposes a separate limit: when the next call reaches a different deployment, cached-context reuse drops from 89% to 29%, and treating KV state as deployment-local raises the recompute floor under unlimited memory from 5.4% to 20.2%. These findings motivate retention that changes the representation of KV state, together with deployment-aware routing or migration. We plan to release AgenticTraceSim, a parametric trace generator, and a residency replay framework.

items.title: Do You Trust Apple?
items.author: Ben Thompson
items.content: Listen to this post: Log in to listen On July 21, 1999, Steve Jobs did something remarkable at Macworld New York: first he went to Apple.com, then to “CNN Interactive”, then to Disney.com. That wasn’t the remarkable part: what blew the crowd away was when he picked up the just-introduced iBook and walked around while waiting for Disney.com to load. The crowd went wild at the lack of wires: I’m not going to quote this entire product introduction, but I’ve clipped the whole thing for your enjoyment; here are a few pertinent parts of Jobs’ introduction of what he called “AirPort”, and what the rest of the industry called “WiFi”: There is one more thing. The main point of this keynote was the aforementioned introduction of the original iBook: This meant that “one more thing” was in fact not just an extra unexpected product, but an explicit addition to the primary product’s feature set. No wire. What is going on here? We are really excited to announce, in addition to iBook, AirPort wireless networking…It’s a wireless LAN. It runs at 11 megabits per second, and it’s based on industry standards. This is 802.11 wireless networking, and everybody is jumping on board with this thing over the next six to nine months. So all sorts of devices are going to be able to interact with AirPorts. We’re just going to be there first and best, and the specification also incorporates quite a bit of privacy protection, so everything you send out is encrypted. A lot of privacy. We’ve worked with Lucent on this for the last 18 months, hand-in-hand to marry their wireless technology with our ease-of-use technology and to bring the cost of this down for people, because this stuff has been pretty pricey to date. Apple’s selling proposition has, in many respects, never changed: modern technology that is easy to use and private too. So AirPort, what is it? This is the first thing: this is the AirPort base station, and it looks like this, right like that, and so the AirPort base station is really cool… And, of course, industrial design: So what about the computer side of things? Well, iBook is the first computer ever designed right from the start to be optimized for wireless communications, and so right in every iBook are two built-in antennas…Then, we have an AirPort card, a small little card, and the iBook is designed to accept it. So let’s take a look at that. As you know, Apple pioneered this way of adding memory without taking your whole portable apart through simply lifting the keyboard. Well, we have enhanced that now to take an AirPort card, and as you see, there’s a space right there in every iBook ready for an AirPort card, and you can drop one in, just like that, and connect the cable that comes from the antenna. Right? You saw that? I’ll go back. Just connect that cable and push it in, and now your iBook is AirPort functioning. You are on the wireless network. All the software detects the AirPort card and automatically sets it up for wireless networking without going through hours of configuring your computer. It all happens automatically. This has been a major effort on the part of Apple’s hardware and software engineers and also Lucent. This paragraph is a bit extraneous, other than the fact it is personally meaningful: my first Apple computer was an iMac G4, the following all-white generation, with the same AirPort card installation. I remember being amazed at just how easy it was to add wireless. And now, here I am, 22 years later, still using an Apple laptop to write this Article. Apple HomeView Two weeks ago I wondered how long I was for the Apple ecosystem; one product I was definitely not interested in was the then-forthcoming Apple smarthome product: What struck me about Gurman’s article is just how unenthused I am by an Apple smarthome product. Some of this is fatigue from a decade of Siri disappointment and skepticism about the company’s ability to deliver on a voice-centric product. More than that, however, I bristle at the idea of introducing Apple’s constraints to more parts of my life. Those constraints aren’t just about things like full disk access. To the extent that Apple delivers on integration with things like thermostats and door locks is the extent to which they work with 3rd-party device makers; the problem is that third party device makers mostly suck, particularly from a software perspective. Even if Siri were perfect, Apple will have the challenge of delivering an experience that isn’t defined by the lowest common denominator. What I’m much more interested in is controlling the software layer myself. The fact of the matter is that with AI you can decompile almost all existing software — there is a revolution happening in gaming over the past few weeks, as game after game is decompiled to source and ported to any platform you wish — and you can write your own. That means my software that interacts with my agent in the way I want it to for everything; that’s way more exciting than praying Apple delivers the right API and that 3rd-party developers don’t suck. That product is called Apple HomeView, and some prominent Apple observers don’t get the point. John Gruber wrote on Daring Fireball: My skepticism boils down to the question of why anyone would want to add one (or more!) additional ever-present screens to our homes and lives. Phones can stay in our pockets until we need them. Watches remain on our wrists. HomePods can be tucked away unobtrusively in corners, and remain fully useful. HomeView needs to be in a prominent location for its display to serve any practical purpose. Apple’s initial pitch for it doesn’t earn that prominence for me. I understand Gruber’s skepticism, particularly given the product’s truly atrocious introductory video. Beyond the overall stress-inducing nature of the suburban family scene depicted, most of the use cases, as Gruber notes, are nonsensical: to take a particularly egregious example, why would the teenage daughter look at a message from her clandestine boyfriend on the HomeView instead of her iPhone (which has to be present on the network and unlocked in the past several hours for that functionality to even work)? Apple was, in this particular case, trying to show off HomeView’s multi-user capability, which is based on facial recognition, but my biggest takeaway is that maybe highly produced marketing videos sold as product keynotes aren’t the worst idea in the world. In fact, I think that HomeView is pretty compelling. Smarthome functionality is genuinely useful: Years ago I set up a small monitor on the side of our condo’s living room for the kids to play video games; I happened to have a Raspberry Pi on hand, which I used to set up a service called DAKboard. DAKboard showed the time, the weather, the family calendar, and a rotating collection of photos. It has, in the intervening years, been one of our most-used and most-beloved pieces of technology, looked at multiple times a day every day. Thermostats are finicky and hard to use; it’s much better to be able to program them from your phone, or from a touch device. The problem for me in my current home is that my thermostats seem to mysteriously lose their connection to my home automation system every few weeks. Doorbells are critical in a world of e-commerce, especially when it comes to the dreaded “signature required”; incorporating them with your devices, along with a screen to see who is at the door, is a no-brainer. Unfortunately for me my doorbells also seem to get randomly disconnected, and I never notice until I miss a delivery. Cameras are a useful security measure, but only if you can actually view them. The issue is — you guessed it — that they often become inaccessible or are non-intuitive to use, particularly the moment you need them. Sometimes I want to access information without using my hands, like when I am cooking. You can prop up an iPhone or iPad in the kitchen, but what do you do when it goes to sleep in the middle of a recipe? I have, of course, just laid out five compelling use cases for the HomeView, but it wasn’t hard! These are all real, genuinely useful capabilities for a new home device. And notice what the limiting factor is for the middle three: actually getting different devices to work together reliably. Apple’s Trust Dividend That’s why the other exciting part about Apple’s HomeView announcement actually hearkened back to the original AirPort: Apple Home Collection. From Apple’s press release: Apple today announced Apple Home Collection, a new lineup of smart home accessories — including indoor and outdoor cameras, thermostats, temperature sensors, and a video doorbell and door lock — designed in collaboration with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. These new accessories are simple to set up starting with one tap with iPhone, and everything is managed through the Apple Home app — no separate app or account required. Each accessory is encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home, so only users and the people they choose can access their home data. Building on the thousands of Works with Apple Home and Matter accessories available today, Apple Home Collection offers customers a new array of recommended products to better understand what’s happening inside and outside their home, manage access, and keep the temperature just right throughout the day. Availability for all products begins in December, with select accessories available starting early 2027. “Apple Home Collection makes it easy to choose smart home accessories with confidence,” said Matthew Costello, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “Working closely with industry leaders LG Electronics and Schneider Electric, we designed every accessory to work seamlessly with Apple Home, so managing your home is simple, reliable, and private.” Apple doesn’t have to do everything itself in the home, just as they didn’t have to invent wireless networking in 1999; what they need to do is “marry [partner’s] technology with [their] ease-of-use technology”, and I’m optimistic they’ve done exactly that with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The key detail is “no separate app or account required”; that points to deep integration with Apple products, from setup to day-to-day usage. Again, I’m not sure I’m the target customer for this (although the automatically unlocking door locks look awesome); my solution to incompatible or flakey integrations is to use AI to build my own customized software. I’m under no illusions, however, that I am a normal consumer who wants the benefits of technology without the headaches; I trust Apple, more than anyone else, to at least aspire to delivering on that vision, and these 2nd-party partnerships are a great start. The second part where you may trust Apple more than any other company is with privacy. Jobs was talking about privacy as a selling point 27 years ago, and Apple has only doubled down since then. In the case of HomeView specifically there is that facial recognition feature, tied to your own hardware; more broadly, if there is any company you might entrust with tracking your more private spaces it is Apple, both because of promises they make with their technology and also their consistent stance on not using customer data. Indeed, Apple’s privacy umbrella is strong enough that LG’s very sketchy privacy track record is likely to be a non-issue amongst potential customers. Apple’s Trust Deficit From Bloomberg, in 2016: Apple Inc. has disbanded its division that develops wireless routers, another move to try to sharpen the company’s focus on consumer products that generate the bulk of its revenue, according to people familiar with the matter. Apple began shutting down the wireless router team over the past year, dispersing engineers to other product development groups, including the one handling the Apple TV, said the people, who asked not to be named because the decision hasn’t been publicly announced. Apple hasn’t refreshed its routers since 2013 following years of frequent updates to match new standards from the wireless industry. The decision to disband the team indicates the company isn’t currently pushing forward with new versions of its routers. An Apple spokeswoman declined to comment on the company’s plans. The official end of the line came in 2018, five years after the last product was released, leaving customers in limbo waiting for updates that never came. That right there is one reason to not trust Apple in the home: the company already decided once that products that didn’t move the needle relative to the iPhone weren’t worth their time, even if delivering an integrated home experience was still something Apple was uniquely positioned to provide. Yes, by the 2010s most people had WiFi access points from their ISPs, or mesh WiFi products from the likes of Eero, but Apple still could have done something useful. For example, one of the biggest challenges in designing a wireless network is that the iPhone aggressively holds onto access points; if Apple had continued to design its own access points it could, even today, provide a superior experience. Alas, the business was deemed to be not big enough to bother. One reason Apple might be more interested this time, however, is the possibility of subscription revenue. Specifically, the cameras in Apple Home Collection will require a paid iCloud+ plan for recorded event history — higher levels for more cameras — which fits in with the company’s focus on services. Apple Music is also natively supported on the HomeView, whereas you’ll need a recently unlocked iPhone to use Spotify. Of course to some this might be another betrayal of trust: Apple used to sell you products, now they want to sell you on-ramps to recurring revenue. Both of these issues of trust, however, pale in comparison to the single biggest question facing HomeView: do you trust Siri to actually work? In Siri We Trust (or Not) From Mark Gurman at Bloomberg: Apple Inc.’s new HomeView has been a long time coming — far longer than the company intended. I first reported on the device in January 2023, when Apple was aiming to bring it to market as early as the end of 2024. What should have been a relatively straightforward launch instead turned into a nearly two-year saga of delays. The culprit was Apple’s AI crisis, which left the company without the one piece of technology the HomeView absolutely needed: a working version of its revamped Siri assistant… From the beginning, the HomeView was built around a Siri that could retrieve personal content, distinguish between members of a household and show each person private information. It was also designed to be controlled primarily by voice, rather than through its touch screen. Without a serviceable version of the new assistant, Apple couldn’t deliver the experience it had envisioned. That left the hardware ready to go, but the software nowhere near finished. So Apple postponed the HomeView repeatedly — first until spring 2025, then summer, then fall, and then again throughout 2026 before finally unveiling it this past week. And the hardware betrays its age. With thick bezels, an A18 processor and 8 gigabytes of memory, this is clearly a product conceived years ago. Finished units have been sitting boxed up in warehouses for the better part of a year, waiting for the software to catch up. There is a world where Apple never gives up on AirPort, and instead uses it as a foundation to deliver the integrated smarthome in the late 2010s; in that world Siri’s performance is important but also less pressing given that some number of homes would already be locked in. The second world, which Gurman describes, is one where Apple delivers on the new Siri in 2024 like it planned, and the HomeView is its showpiece experience. This is still a compelling product in that scenario, where integrating information from your iPhone is close to the cutting edge of what AI is capable of. The world we are in in 2026, however, is a much different one. In this world Siri AI has shipped, and while it is more capable than what came before, it is much slower, and makes more mistakes with basic tasks that the deterministic old Siri handled reliably. Moreover, the competitive landscape is dramatically different: agents like Muse, Instinct, Dots, or Grok Bots not only integrate information but actually act on it; new Siri already feels long in the tooth. This is where a foray into the home is particularly challenging. One doesn’t replace one’s thermostat or cameras or doorbells every year; these are one-time purchases meant to last for a long time. Ditto cutting a hole in your wall to mount a HomeView, which certainly makes more sense for many of the product’s core use cases. Making such a commitment, however, means committing to Siri AI as the primary interface, and trusting that Apple will make it good. This is a costly choice, and not just monetarily. The real concern is opportunity cost: committing to a world controlled by Siri AI means forgoing a world controlled by any other AI. That’s too expensive for me; how many consumers, even those who trust Apple to make things work together, and who value the company’s commitment to privacy, will make a similar evaluation? Cook’s Costs The answer right now, in 2026, is probably not too many, which is to say Apple might have got this product out just in time. I think there is something here, even if Apple’s marketing team doesn’t seem to be able to explain it very well. At the same time, I think HomeView highlights some of the mistakes and shortcomings of former CEO Tim Cook’s tenure; earlier this year when Cook retired I wrote about his impeccable timing, both in terms of when he took over Apple, and also when he stepped down: To that end, it’s right that Cook is stepping down now. Jobs might have been responsible for taking Apple from 0 to 1, but it was Cook that took Apple from 1 to $436 billion in revenue and $118 billion in profit last year. It’s a testament to his capabilities and execution that Apple didn’t suffer any sort of post-founder hangover; only time will tell if, along the way, Cook created the conditions for a crash out, by virtue of he himself forgetting The Cook Doctrine and what makes Apple Apple. The Cook Doctrine states that Apple needs “to own and control the primary technologies behind the products we make”, but Apple doesn’t own and control the models underlying Siri; meanwhile, one of the things that makes Apple Apple is focusing on making great products that customers love. How did Apple’s obsession with services revenue fit in that rubric, particularly when said obsession rose in conjunction with stripping out every part of the business that didn’t move the needle in terms of revenue, even if it made for a better user experience? Privacy, meanwhile, is great as a strategy credit; what happens when it gets in the way of making products that work? It is true that Apple’s AI approach has the benefit of not moving the needle in terms of costs, at least relative to its big tech peers. It’s possible that just as Apple is partnering with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric on home devices, the company will deliver compelling experiences through its partnership with Google (and surprising thawing with Meta via its Meta Superintelligence Lab). After all, Apple hasn’t always done everything — Lucent Technologies once featured in a Steve Jobs keynote! The difference is that that was an Apple that was eager to race ahead, not simply catch up; Jobs was planting seeds for the future, seeds that Cook harvested. Cook did make investments that matter, particularly in Apple Silicon (even if that effort started under Jobs), and in wearables; the job for Ternus will be ensuring that Apple’s “ease-of-use” technology is not just easy but actually useful.

items.title: The FDE Bubble: Silicon Valley’s Most Expensive Game Of Pretend
items.author: Guest Author
items.content: By Anurag Gurtu Congratulations to the enterprise AI company that just raised another nine-figure round to solve a problem software is supposed to solve by itself: getting humans to use the product. You know the one. Won’t name it. Don’t have to. You’ve read the press release — “autonomous,” “agentic,” “category-defining” in paragraph one, and then, a few paragraphs down, where the money is actually going: hiring an army of engineers to sit inside customer offices and manually make the “autonomous” thing behave. Nothing says “we’ve built the future of work” quite like raising half a billion dollars to hire more people to do the work. The business model, decoded Anurag Gurtu, co-founder and CEO of Airrived. Here’s how it works, in case the deck was too artfully vague: Sell the customer an “AI platform.” Discover the platform doesn’t actually do the thing on its own. Send in the forward deployed engineers: sharp young people with CS degrees who now spend six months hand-building the workflow the website implied already existed. Bill the customer for “software.” Book it as ARR. Raise a bigger round because “ARR go up.” Repeat, forever, with an increasingly large and increasingly expensive engineering org standing between the product and the promise it made. This is not a flywheel. This is a payroll with a pitch deck. And the industry has stopped even pretending otherwise — it’s fundraising on it, loudly. OpenAI pledged up to $1.5 billion into a deployment joint venture valued at $10 billion, with another $4 billion from TPG, Bain Capital, Advent, Brookfield and Goanna. The vehicle, DeployCo, has been reported with more than $4 billion in investment. Meanwhile, job postings for “forward deployed engineer” are up somewhere between 800% and 1,000% year over year. Lightcast data reported by Fortune put the increase at more than 1,000% from January to August 2026. Financial Times data carried by PYMNTS put listings up more than 800% from January to September 2025, and Indeed data showed postings rising from 643 in April 2025 to 5,330 in April 2026. Total comp is pushing past $300,000 in the U.S. Employer postings list Anthropic at $280,000 to $320,000 base pay and OpenAI at $185,000 to $300,000 base, plus equity. Fortune reported some Anthropic roles reaching $400,000 in total compensation. Somewhere, a VC is calling this “operating leverage” with a completely straight face. It is not operating leverage. It’s a staffing agency that learned to say “agentic.” The tell Ask the one question the pitch deck conveniently never answers: “If you pulled the embedded engineer out tomorrow, does the customer still get what they paid for?” If the honest answer is “well, no, but the ARR is real” — that’s not product-market fit. That’s people-market fit, and people-market fit has a brutally unglamorous ceiling: You can only hire humans so fast, and you can never hire them cheap enough to earn a software multiple. Every new logo doesn’t get more profitable to serve. It gets another headcount request. Two companies, same $20 million ARR. One needs 10 engineers to keep the lights on. The other needs 100. Both slides say, “AI software company.” The difference shows up in gross margin, cost to onboard the next customer, and whether that cost falls as the company scales. The bill always comes due Here’s the thing about people-market fit: it feels great right up until someone asks the unfashionable questions: What does it actually cost, fully loaded, to onboard the next customer? Does that number go down as the company scales, or does it just grow the org chart? What happens to gross margin if the first year growth slows and the headcount can’t hide behind hypergrowth anymore? Companies funding their FDE armies with fresh nine-figure rounds are betting nobody asks these questions until after the round closes and the confetti is swept up. That’s a fine bet in a hype cycle. It’s a terrible one in a market that’s about to start reading the fine print. Because eventually, someone always reads the fine print. A CFO builds a cost-per-deployment model. A CIO benchmarks time-to-value against three vendors instead of trusting one demo. An investor finally does the unglamorous work of separating software ARR from human-powered ARR on the same balance sheet. The distinction buyers and investors can test is on the numbers. Software ARR should get cheaper to deliver as it scales. Human-powered ARR does not. OpenAI guaranteed the private-equity backers of its deployment vehicle an annual 17.5% return over five years, which is a different structure from a growth thesis.¹ So no, your AI isn’t autonomous. But your business model might be — autonomously transferring the cost of a services company onto a software valuation, for as long as the music plays. Enjoy the round. Hope the org chart was worth it. Anurag Gurtu, the co-founder and CEO of Airrived, is an entrepreneur and product leader with more than 20 years of experience across cybersecurity and AI. He has built three generative AI companies, including one that reached unicorn status. Gurtu is known for turning advanced AI into scalable, real-world platforms, and previously contributed to successful exits, including acquisitions by Splunk, Tripwire and Sun Microsystems, and a public company, FireEye. He holds a master’s degree from the University of Southern California and CISSP certification. Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: LatAm Startup Funding Jumps 26% In Q3 As VCs Begin ‘Rediscovering’ The Region
items.author: Judy Rider
items.content: A continued boom in late-stage and growth funding combined with a surge in seed-stage funding helped buoy venture investment in Latin America for the third quarter of 2026, Crunchbase data shows. All told, startups in Latin America raised a combined $1.3 billion across seed- and growth-stage deals in the three-month period ending Sept. 30. That was up 26% year over year but down 9% from the second quarter. For perspective, we charted out total investment, color-coded by stage, for the past 12 quarters below. Of the quarterly total, $757 million went into late-stage and growth deals, up 74% compared to the $435 million that flowed into such deals in the third quarter of 2025. However, that is down 21.3% from the $962 million in late-stage and growth rounds raised by LatAm startups in the second quarter. (Although it’s worth noting that Q2 2026 represented the most raised at that stage since the second quarter of 2022.) Mexico startups have raised $1.52 billion in venture funding during the first three quarters of 2026, per Crunchbase data. Notably, that’s about 40.7% more than the $1.08 billion Brazil’s startups raised in the same period. This is unusual as Brazil has historically been the largest recipient of venture funding in Latin America. Still, Brazil continues to attract a broad range of investors. “Over the past year, we have seen investments into Brazil from firms including Sequoia, Founders Fund, NEA, Battery and Tidemark,” Allen Taylor, managing partner of Endeavor Catalyst, told Crunchbase News. “For several, this marked either their first investment in Latin America or their first in a long time.” Igor Piquet, Endeavor Catalyst’s vice president and head of Latin America, noted that Mexico drew more venture funding in the first half of 2026 than Brazil. But much of Mexico’s funding went to a few startups, he pointed out, while Brazil recorded many deals. “Investors are concentrating on a few Mexican winners, while Brazil retains the breadth,” Piquet said, adding that Brazil also leads in realized exits. Table of contents Outsized rounds An uptick in seed funding ‘Another rediscovery moment’ Methodology Glossary of funding terms Outsized rounds Several mega-raises took place in Latin America in the third quarter. And notably, the two largest funding deals were not for companies in Brazil or Mexico, which have historically raised the largest share of venture capital in the region. They also weren’t to fintech, which typically has the most funding recipients in the region, but rather to energy-related startups. Black Giant, the Chilean project company for EnergyX’s Black Giant lithium project, raised $225 million in a July round at a reported $900 million valuation. And Colombia’s Erco Energía, a clean energy company that builds and operates solar power systems for homes and businesses, landed a $129 million Series C in August at a reported $600 million valuation. Mexico’s Kapital, an AI-powered financial services company, raised a $125 million Series C in September at a $1.6 billion valuation. Tru Arrow Partners and Fasanara Capital co-led the financing. And in August, Brazilian fintech Kesh Bank brought in $106.9 million in an equity and debt seed round at a $626 million valuation. Also in August, Brazil’s Decade, an AI-native wealth advisory company, landed $85 million in what Crunchbase data shows is the largest seed funding deal ever raised for a Latin American startup. Founded by Vitor Olivier, former CTO of Nubank, and Felipe Meneses, founder of Hyperplane AI, the startup is backed by Benchmark, Greenoaks, Diffusion, Norte Ventures and Atlantico. An uptick in seed funding Latin America experienced a marked surge in very early-stage funding totals in the third quarter, largely thanks to the seed rounds mentioned above. Of the $1.3 billion raised by Latin America’s startups in the third quarter, about 20.5% — or $266 million — was raised across the angel and seed stages. That’s up 128% from the $117 million raised across those stages in the second quarter of 2026, and up 62% from the $165 million in the same quarter last year. Just over 22%, or $288 million, was raised at early stages, down 18.9% from $355 million in the second quarter and 34% from $437 million in the same period last year. We expect the Q3 deal counts to rise somewhat over time; however, as seed rounds in particular are commonly reported weeks or months after they close. ‘Another rediscovery moment’ Latin America is drawing renewed interest from international venture investors, according to Endeavor’s Taylor. He said international VCs were more active in the region, particularly Brazil, during the first three quarters of 2026 than in 2024 and 2025 combined, through both new investments and follow-on funding. “I joke that investors from the U.S. ‘rediscover’ Latin America every five or six years, and I think we are approaching another rediscovery moment,” Taylor told Crunchbase News. Endeavor Catalyst recently closed its oversubscribed $320 million fifth fund. Latin America accounts for nearly 40% of its portfolio by both deals and dollars, and Fund V had made 14 investments in the region as of Sept. 22. Taylor also pointed to opportunities beyond Brazil and Mexico, including repeat founders building global businesses from Colombia and emerging companies in Venezuela and Central America. Liquidity is improving, although acquisitions and secondary transactions are providing more opportunities than public listings, Piquet said. He pointed to approximately 60 private Latin American technology companies that have each raised at least $150 million as a potential pipeline for future IPOs. “The exit door is open, although it is not primarily opening through IPOs yet,” Piquet said. Taylor expects more exits could help bring global investors back consistently, with potential New York Stock Exchange listings by companies such as Wellhub, CloudWalk or Creditas contributing to another “rediscovery moment” in 2027. International investors remain interested in Latin America but have become more selective about deploying capital, according to Ana Cristina Gadala-Maria of QED Investors. Firms with a longstanding presence in the region remain engaged, while many that entered during the 2020–2021 investment boom have shifted toward AI opportunities elsewhere and are concentrating on existing portfolios, she noted. “Global investors are increasingly investing behind themes rather than geographies,” she said, putting Latin American startups in more direct competition with companies in the U.S. and other markets. Investor interest is increasingly centered on AI-native businesses and financial infrastructure, particularly stablecoins and cross-border payments. Gadala-Maria said more founders are targeting global markets from the outset, marking a departure from the previous wave of startups that adapted established business models to underserved local markets. “Increasingly, we’re seeing founders build globally competitive technology companies from Latin America, rather than necessarily for Latin America,” she said. Gadala-Maria agrees that Brazil and Mexico remain the region’s largest markets, with Brazil offering a deeper, more mature startup ecosystem and Mexico providing substantial room for financial services innovation. She pointed to Argentina as an overlooked market, citing its strong technical talent and founders building companies for global customers. Related Crunchbase queries: Latin America Venture Funding In 2026 Largest LatAm Seed & Pre-Seed Rounds 2000-Q3 2026 Methodology The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Oct. 5, 2026. Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year. Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price. Glossary of funding terms Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less. Early-stage consists of Series A and Series B rounds, as well as other round types. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million. Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round. Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.) Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: Stratospheric airship flew from US to Japan to test sky cell tower concept
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.content: Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey's length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky. The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock. “We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we're twice as high as air traffic and we're above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen, founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we're still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content: Interesting research: Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch. For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first. Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on. Neither improves with exposure. We study what changes when a solver improves with use. Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access. It reaches 85.4% overall and 84.2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone. Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation. The same loop also repairs it. A CAPTCHA operator can perturb images against the publicly released detector and drive its accuracy to 0%, but the perturbations leave VLM untouched, and its labels let the detector recover. Under a year-long simulated arms race in which the CAPTCHA operator re-crafts its perturbations each month, the solver recovers every round, and a cheap ~70%-accurate open-weight teacher hardens it as effectively as a perfect oracle. Visual CAPTCHA defenses that assume a failing bot stays failing therefore understate how quickly an adaptive solver returns.
