items.title: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun
items.author: Jack Clark
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now Here’s a speech I gave on Saturday the 17th of October at the IMF meeting in Bangkok. This speech is inspired by the megatrend readers have seen me cover this year of AI beginning to operate at the frontier of human science, sometimes autonomously. While we all may quibble over the details, I think it’s evident we’re in the early stages of the singularity, and I wanted to use my privileged position of giving the Per Jacobsson lecture to try and tell the assembled audience of economists, bankers, and policymakers, that they should expect significant, rapid change in the future. In this speech, I focused primarily on how humanity can share in the benefits of AI if we exercise proper foresight and restraint, and I’m going to be expanding on the stakes of the singularity and the risks that we’ll all face in coming issues. As I said a few times in the speech – some of which was ad libbed and not captured here – I take my own responsibility here extremely seriously. I find myself both a narrator of what is happening in AI, a principle agent behind what is happening in AI, and a translator that goes between many communities. In all of this, I am seeking to be truthful and to be clear about my own culpability. This is a forever work-in-progress. Thank you all for reading. Speeches like this draw heavily from the newsletter, and the newsletter is my attempt to provide week-by-week information to all of you. I appreciate your readership. *** Inside the Event Horizon: Why Everyone Should Take AI Progress Seriously Hello, thank you for having me. It is a great privilege to be here. To start, I should list my relevant credentials: I am a human being. There is one of me. It has taken me almost 40 years to build the experience to give this speech. I will come back to those credentials later. My whole career has been defined by finding information that seemed important to the future of the world, then telling the world about that information.Two decades ago, I started my career as a journalist, focusing on data centers. Through that work, I became so obsessed with AI that in 2016 I left journalism to work at OpenAI, then co-founded Anthropic a few years later. Ever since, I’ve been trying to convince the world that one day, AI systems might become so powerful that they could alter national security, change the economic trajectory of the planet, and perhaps eventually gain the ability to build themselves. Well, the moment has arrived. AI is now changing national security, it is altering the economic trajectory of the world – as we’ve heard in so many sessions here – and is contributing to its own development. Of course, many of you know this, and you are having to track AI as one of a multitude of destabilizing forces that is shaping your world and your work. What I am here to explain today is that AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly. And I’m going to explain why. For many years, researchers and science fiction authors have forecast a future in which AI systems drastically increase the pace of overall scientific and technical progress, making things move so quickly that it is hard for humans to keep up. They call this the singularity. I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun. The writer Vernor Vinge forecast this in 1993. “When greater-than-human intelligence drives progress, that progress will be much more rapid. In fact, there seems no reason why progress itself would not involve the creation of still more intelligent entities — on a still-shorter time scale,” he wrote, describing the singularity as “a point where our models must be discarded and a new reality rules.” The singularity is here. The implications reach across every aspect of life. But the most important implication is a simple one: we should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up. This will feel confusing and disorienting, and it will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril. Today, I’m going to concentrate on the first point: the potential benefits of rapid AI progress, and what we need to do to share in these benefits together. So many of the ways that humanity will benefit from AI come from science. I believe that AI-driven scientific invention will change the course of the global economy, alter the ways countries plan and build their own infrastructure, make us all healthier and able to spend more time with our loved ones, and –– at the same time –– cause us all to ask deep philosophical questions about choices we should make about its continued development. I’ll develop my claim: For the last half century, most countries have dealt with falling research productivity while researcher headcount grows rapidly – ideas and inventions appear to be getting harder to find. But something important has changed: we’ve now built AI systems which have been able to augment, extend, and automate aspects of human labor. This has most obviously happened in software development, where AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers. As a consequence, the field of software development is changing – A single person is now able to write software for anything they can imagine, creating things that previously would have taken entire teams of humans. We’ve seen concrete evidence of this inside Anthropic, where our researchers now produce almost 10 times the amount of code than they did for the first four years of the company’s life. But new AI capabilities bring new challenges – the coding improvements have meant AI systems have got much better at cybersecurity and cyberattacks –– leading the world to race to deploy these powerful capabilities to create better cyberdefenses, while bad actors race to use these systems to carry out hacks. The important thing to notice here is that these things are bound up, inseparably – the advance of AI systems in a general area like coding has also created both positive and negative impacts in domains of international relevance, like cybersecurity. This is a taste of things to come. Of progress yielding new capabilities, and new challenges. These capabilities will not stop at coding; the same thing will happen to science and robotics. It has already begun to happen. And it means some important properties of the global economy may change – like the rate of innovation, or the frequency with which we invent entirely new general purpose technologies that create new industries around themselves, like the internet, phones, and artificial intelligence. So, what causes me to believe this? In 2026, we have got the first signs that AI systems may be capable of doing science at the frontier, and we have some evocative examples of what the future could look like. For instance: In mathematics, AI systems have been used to propose solutions to longstanding mathematical problems, like the Navier Stokes Millenium Prize, the Jacobian Conjecture, and several open Erdos problems. In many cases, AI systems were responsible for core insights that made the solution possible. In biology, researchers have used AI to design viruses from scratch, to identify new drug candidates for testing, and there are already drugs in trials today which have been in large part designed by AI. In robotics, AI systems are now increasingly able to autonomously operate laboratory equipment remotely, making it possible for us to further automate experimentation in domains from biology to materials science, making progress faster in areas like batteries and fuel-cell development. Taken individually, each of these examples is exciting. But the profound fact is that they all relate to the same underlying technology – and for most of these use-cases, the same single underlying frontier model. We now have singular entities – AI systems like Claude or ChatGPT or Gemini – which can carry out work at the frontier of multiple scientific disciplines. Quantitative metrics bear this out. One such metric is the score of AI systems at a test called Humanity’s Last Exam – I didn’t choose the name! This ominously named test was developed in response to the profound advances seen in prior years by AI systems at a variety of difficult and varied scientific challenges, covering topics as varied as advanced chemistry, computer science, mathematics, classical literature, and ecology. When the exam launched in January 2025, top scoring AI systems obtained a score of 8%. As of this week, the highest scoring system is Claude Opus 5.5 with 67.7%. Another example is FrontierMath, a test released in November 2024 that sought to assess how well AI systems could solve hundreds of challenging math problems, curated and evaluated by professional mathematicians. When it launched, the best scoring systems got 2%. Now, they get 94%. More broadly, it looks like this everywhere. Pick your favorite part of science and go looking for a test and you’ll find this pattern – sudden and steep increases in capability, everywhere you look. TheoPhysEval I’ll close my evidence with a story. The latest example comes to us from a paper published just last week, called TheoPhysEval. This is a paper that tests out how well AI systems can solve unpublished problems in theoretical physics. The 50 questions in the paper were compiled by physicists around the world. Unsurprisingly, AI systems got high scores. But what is surprising is how they got the high scores. Here, I am going to quote from Indian physicist Suvrat Raju, who wrote a post commenting on the results. “I don’t know of any individual who can solve any significant fraction of our final collection of problems without AI assistance,” he said. “Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5. But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).” Think about this for a moment. Some of the world’s scientific experts built a test out of problems an AI could never have possibly read the answer to. And when they tested the AI, not only did it score high, but it got a higher score by finding errors in the answers that the humans had worked on! There is a scene in films, usually two thirds of the way through, when the young protagonist finally proves to their mentor that they have what it takes to go out into the world and succeed independently. It is a narrative trope – when the teacher becomes the student. That is what is happening here. So, why am I telling you this? Why does it matter that AI systems are getting better at science? I believe it is because doing true frontier science – being capable of making breakthroughs that extend the frontier of knowledge – implicitly tests for one of the last frontiers of AI capability: creativity. My view is that if AI systems can creatively problem solve to succeed at science, we should expect this to be a sign of their ability to generalize into many domains, including certainly AI research itself, which could have an explosive effect on innovation. Therefore, if AI systems get better at science, this will strongly drive the growth and shape of the future economy, which means that you can make decisions today to set up your nations and people to benefit from this trend in the future. Science and growth Let’s talk about growth. One of the main sources of growth is in research yielding new ideas. One of the things that drives growth is our stock of human capital – the people all over the world who ask questions and conduct scientific research and thus help the world move forward. But we also know that, as some economists have said, “good ideas are getting harder to find.” The cost of breakthroughs is going up, and we’ve had to pour an ever-rising amount of resources into research to keep going at the same pace. What if this changed? With this technology, we can fundamentally change both the number of researchers on the planet, and how long it takes to train them. As I said at the beginning, when I listed my credentials, there is one of me and it took me about 40 years to get here. What would it mean to be able to run hundreds or thousands of copies of me simultaneously? What would it mean if new versions of me could be created instantly, rather than waiting 40 years? How would my work change if I could make copies of myself and order them to do work under my supervision? That is what the next few years will be like for large swathes of the economy – we will be able to augment human labor in frontier disciplines, like science, in a way we’ve never been able to do before. This will likely change the rate at which we find good ideas, because we’ll be able to add 100s or 1000s of times as many researchers to any problem, force multiplying our human scientists. We can also do this very quickly. If you wanted to train a new generation of researchers in a certain area, it might take you 10 or 15 years of targeted education, and millions of dollars, to even get a small cohort. On the other hand, these AI systems can be created immediately, in arbitrary numbers, as long as there is enough computing capacity – and they can be used across domains to benefit from new scientific insights near instantaneously, and they can combine existing knowledge in new and surprising ways to make discoveries. This means that we can rapidly augment humans in domains that show promise by generating large amounts of virtual scientists to work alongside them. This means that in the coming years, every human scientist on this planet will become more important and more powerful, as they gain the ability to supervise hundreds or thousands of like-minded experts on any problem they find interesting. We have done some of our own modeling here, where we have tried to simulate different versions of the economy according to different trajectories of the technology. If you assume that models will be able to autonomously complete a broad range of tasks and will diffuse quickly in the economy, then under these singularity-esque conditions, we could see an unprecedented economic transformation, with US GDP reaching 44 trillion by 2030. This sounds outlandish, but it’s implicated by the technology continuing to get better. If GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such major economic expansion – and that is exactly what is implied by this notion of having AI systems be capable of autonomous scientific inquiry. So, what do we do about this? How do we set up the world broadly to benefit from these advancing capabilities? How do we balance this opportunity for progress with appropriate caution? We need to both plan for success so that humanity can take advantage of this technology and use it to create abundance, and be prepared to make wise choices about how to use the technology itself – just because AI will be a capable scientist, that does not mean we should use it for absolutely everything. On planning for success, I’ll start with a story from my own experience. For the last ten years, I have gone to governments around the world and tried to convey a very simple but important fact: that AI systems are getting far more powerful and useful, and that these systems require large amounts of computers. Therefore, I said, the single best thing a government could do to position itself to take advantage of the AI revolution was to build enough electricity capacity and data center space to be able to host the kinds of powerful AI systems discussed here, and to invest in the AI supply chain. Not many policymakers listened. Now, we deal with the consequences of that. In today’s world, data center capacity is concentrated in the United States, China, and increasingly the Middle East, and the supply chains are concentrated and are under such contention that prices are going up. That buildout remains important, but it was just the first phase of this economic and scientific revolution implied by AIs continued advance. Now, there is more to be built, and I believe more countries can participate in this – if they choose to. The next phase of the AI revolution is about the expansion into the physical world, specifically by having AI systems increasingly operate robots, and to perform scientific experimentation, sometimes together. Therefore, just as we did with compute and power, we will want to use much more scientific equipment and robotic systems or we will run very quickly out of capacity. We must build this capacity now to let us take maximum advantage of converting this boom in science into benefits for us all. According to estimates by UNESCO, there are approximately ~10 million scientists in the world. Even with only 10 million scientists, we have too few human scientists to oversee the work, too few laboratories to do materials science analysis, too few biological labs to develop and test new drugs, and too few large pieces of scientific equipment in space or on the earth for the experiments we want to run. What happens when instead of ~10 million scientists, we have a billion virtual scientists directed by our own ten million? Or ten billion? That is the world that is coming right for us. We have to get ready. If we do get ready, we are going to be in a better position to translate the intelligence of AI systems into gains for us all: longer, healthier lives, more energy, more food, more wealth. And just as with the data centers, the nations which build and develop this supply chain, will be the ones that will benefit the most. This is an opportunity for everyone: if you are a developed country with a rich scientific ecosystem, you have an opportunity to make all of your scientists more productive. If you are a developing country that supplies the basic ingredients into the AI and scientific enterprise, like raw materials, then you have an opportunity to leapfrog: you can both build scientific testing facilities that, paired with human scientists and digital AI scientists, will let you grow a scientific community, and continue to develop your contribution to the supply chain, which will become more valuable in the future. But infrastructure alone will not be enough. If discovery becomes abundant, we need to avoid bottlenecking ourselves downstream – an avalanche of new proposed drugs is of little use if only a handful can ever be tested. The policymakers and their colleagues in this room will need to help us find ways to accelerate our ability to move discoveries out of the lab and into the clinic, the factory, and the field. The better we prepare for this world, the better able we will be to translate the gains of AI to gains for the world. We also need to prepare ourselves as a global community to make choices about the future. Because as I have said, there is risk here. Being able to use AI for science, opens us up to the misuses of science as well – biological and cyber weapons, and things we can not yet imagine. We have many choices to make, and it’s only by recognizing this technology for what it is – for how powerful it is – that we will see the urgency behind making these choices. The first choice is about where we should direct this technology. Just because we have an AI system that can do science, that doesn’t mean that it should be left to do science unattended. One such use case is biological research, where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety. Another is AI research itself, where labs like Anthropic will need to make decisions about how much oversight we apply to AI-driven research. This could let us make more progress on the technology but also introduces risks. We will need to move extremely carefully here, because otherwise we could lose control of the technology. We will also likely need rules to govern this. I was in Tokyo earlier this week, and a student at a university there said they worked in the physics department, and they said AI was already beginning to be able to do many experiments. What experiments should they spend time on as a person, and what experiments should they let the AI system do itself? This is a subtle question to which I don’t know the answer, but it is a question each discipline of science will need to answer. The second choice is about how much we need to understand about what these AI systems do. As we have seen this year with the rise of AI in mathematics, we are already dealing with a world where the advances made by AI systems are sufficiently creative that we as humans are now spending time trying to decode them – trying to understand what they mean and how to apply these insights for ourselves. How much should we understand? Again, the answer here is going to be subtle, and it relates to fundamental questions of meaning in the age of the singularity – for what parts of scientific progress do we want to have true understanding? We are only a few short years from AI systems not only doing science, but inventing their own new scientific equipment built for the ways AI systems work, rather than human minds. Do we need to understand that equipment? Should we? This is another choice we will need to make. Most importantly, taking AI’s progress seriously means we should give ourselves license to imagine a fundamentally different world When I was a teenager, I read a lot about the world, and I was afraid. I believed that the 21st century was going to be difficult – that population growth, climate change, resource extraction, and other crises would add up to cause a malthusian collapse of the human species. That after rising to invent computers and the internet, we might consume ourselves into the ground. And then over the subsequent years, I saw time and time again how technology could allow us to fundamentally alter these odds: how solar panels came along and became much cheaper, much faster than people expected. How our growing understanding of the human body allowed us to invent cures for things that had killed many people – including some of my own family. How we could do things I had never even imagined but find utterly amazing, like how we are now using AI systems to decode the speech of animals, or how companies have built rockets that take off and then land back on this planet. I work on AI because it can help us do more of that. I work on AI because whether it does that is about choices we make – choices people here in this room will make – about how we direct it and how we govern it. Choices I need to make. I work on AI because it is the most important technology our species has built. It is a technology that, if we are able to use correctly, will let us deal with problems that might otherwise doom us as a species. But it is also a technology that has danger woven into it. For us to get through this – to chart a course through the singularity – we are going to need to work together to create unusual and serious rules for this technology and the companies building it, and to exercise the hardest and I think most noble quality of people – restraint. We will need to build the infrastructure to take advantage of this technology, but we will also need to go slowly and deliberately on developing the technology itself, to pace or otherwise control its development. We need to constantly differentiate between the things we can do and the things we should do. And we will need to invest today in the scientific capabilities to make that progress possible. I am reminded in all of this by the great Carl Sagan, who said in The Pale Blue Dot, that the humans who may one day reach other stars, will be “a species very like us, but with more of our strengths and fewer of our weaknesses… more confident, farseeing, capable, and prudent.” That is what AI demands from us. And where Sagan thought we had hundreds of thousands of years to achieve this – to become a better and wiser people – we instead have a handful of years. I believe we can do it. But it is only by treating AI with the seriousness it deserves that we will succeed. Thank you. Watch the lecture here:

items.title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
items.author: Tim Stevens
items.content: Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift. For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced, and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro. But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front. That's right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement. Read full article Comments

items.title: Wyze moved the screen on its new smart scale to the handle so it’s easier to read at eye level
items.author: Andrew Liszewski
items.content: The scale features a conductive indium tin oxide (ITO) coated glass surface so it can take BIA measurements no matter where your feet are positioned. | Image: Wyze Wyze announced a new version of its Ultra BodyScan smart scale that debuted nearly a year ago with additional electrodes on a retractable handle, allowing it to provide a breakdown of various health metrics across your arms, legs, and torso. With the new Ultra BodyScan Plus, Wyze is introducing a redesign that moves the scale's 4.3-inch customizable color screen to the retractable handle so all the measurements are now displayed closer to eye level. The Wyze Scale Ultra BodyScan Plus is available starting today for $149 through Wyze's online store in black or white color options. That makes it about $30 more expensive than the $119.98 Ultra … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
items.author: Grant Bourzikas
items.content: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update. If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls. This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server? Citrix released software updates to address the flaw, and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch. Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth, to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue. Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform. The NetScaler exploit Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks. CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771. In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow. The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection. Put the access decision in front of the authentication server The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare Access can enforce an independent access policy before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page. That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next. This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero: reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications. Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication. The origin connection must enforce the same boundary Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. It’s important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture. Cloudflare Tunnel is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you won’t have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone. When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example, Dedicated CDN Egress IPs give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application server’s firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makes the network restriction specific to the account's traffic, rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges. Authenticated Origin Pulls can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection. An origin that supports it can also validate the Access JSON Web Token, including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access. If you're unsure where to start, speak with a Cloudflare expert to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment. Protect the web-facing authentication service Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare's web application firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldn’t be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures. Alongside managed CVE signatures, WAF Attack Score uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feed Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform. Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can also use live threat indicators in WAF policies. That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself. Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you haven’t, and follow Citrix's suspected-compromise guidance. They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state. Extend Zero Trust to desktop access, or remove the desktop dependency Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone. Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads, Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client. If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop. Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration. Decide which authentication services need to be public The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone. Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default. Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment: Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin. Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application. Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy. Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work. Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed. Bring the controls together The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic. Get started Speak with a Cloudflare expert to plan the right controls for your environment. Download the solution brief and sign up for the upcoming webinar. Andrei Migia, Nathan Sackett, and Doug Shepherd contributed to this post.

items.title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
items.content: With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible. The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise ~1 million GPUs. Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently. Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people. Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models, including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it. Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind. https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_Video_v1.mp4 The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center. The Supercluster: Unlocking New AI Capabilities Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine. This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep. Multiple Generations of AI Hardware Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric. Catalina: NVIDIA GB200 Our first platform, Catalina, leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100. It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP). The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. We chose Ariel because the GB200 NVL72 scaled up nearly every other dimension relative to the NVIDIA H100: FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, scale-up bandwidth, and scale-up domain size, while scale-out bandwidth per GPU would have stayed at 400G. We expected that imbalance to cost performance, so we opted for a configuration that delivers 800G of scale-out per GPU. This also gave us more uniformity of spec as the region expanded over time and 800G scale-out became available. https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_GB200_GIF_v1.mp4 The Catalina GB200 NVL72 features: 72 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with 13.4 TB of HBM3e (192 GB per GPU). 720 peak PFLOPS of FP8 training compute (1,440 PFLOPS at FP4). 130 TB/s peak NVLink bandwidth within the domain. 576 TB/s peak aggregate memory bandwidth. ~120 kW total system power across the two-rack pair. Clemente: NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 Our second platform, Clemente, moves to the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and improves on Catalina at both the GPU and the platform level. GB300 raises HBM capacity per GPU by 1.5x, from 192 GB to 288 GB, and dense FP4 throughput by a similar factor, while roughly doubling attention (softmax) acceleration. At the platform level, scale-out is no longer the constraint it was on the GB200 NVL72: NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNICs deliver 800G per GPU natively, so the capability we deployed early on Ariel becomes the baseline. That, together with a 2:1 GPU-to-CPU ratio, allows Clemente to pack the full 72-GPU domain into a single rack, streamlining our physical deployment. Clemente can be deployed with our modular Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) or use Facility Liquid Cooling (FLC) in our newly designed data centers. Serviceability also improves substantially, with reduced cabling. https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_GB300_GIF_v1.mp4 The Clemente GB300 NVL72 features: 72 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs with 20.7 TB of HBM3e (288 GB per GPU — 50% more than the GB200). Over 1 exaFLOP of peak FP4 compute. 130 TB/s peak NVLink bandwidth (1.8 TB/s bidirectional per GPU). ~135 kW rack power. 5-10% performance improvement over the GB200 NVL72. Connecting the Supercluster In traditional web services, the data center network transports requests and responses between services whose instances typically don’t require high bandwidth, high performance, and tight, lock-step coordination across many servers. Large-scale AI training requires all these, meaning the network that connects them is now an important part of AI workloads. To best address this, in addition to the standard data center network connecting servers, several years ago we added a second dedicated data network based on Ethernet, called the Back-End (BE) network, to enable direct GPU-to-GPU communication both within and across data center buildings. Large pre-training jobs partition the training into data-parallel model replicas, creating a hierarchy in network usage: Latency-sensitive and bandwidth-sensitive operations concentrate within a replica, while traffic that is more tolerant of higher latency and less bandwidth is scheduled between replicas. Our network is designed to match this hierarchy, with low-latency, high-bandwidth fabrics within buildings and an aggregation network connecting the building fabrics. We work closely with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure the parallelism design, traffic patterns, and communication algorithms and software are optimized to minimize exposure of any network communication. This keeps the GPUs as busy as possible and not waiting on the network. The Meta team has employed these networking concepts in earlier building-scale, 24K GPU clusters and our region-scale, 100K+ GPU cluster over the last several years, and we took them to a new level of scale and distance in Prometheus. Network Fabrics At the building level, each Ethernet-based fabric interconnects up to 20,736 GPUs through a high-bandwidth, low-latency multi-layer topology. Our initial design used a Disaggregated Scheduled Fabric (DSF) to mitigate the network congestion caused by training collectives that typically have a small number of large, long-lived network flows that collide under traditional load-balancing techniques; it does this by utilizing sub-packet-level multipath routing and packet re-ordering in the fabric along with virtual output queues and credit-based end-to-end flow control. As Ethernet NIC technology advanced, enabling packet re-ordering at the endpoint, we were able to update to a Non-Scheduled Fabric (NSF) utilizing shallow-buffer 51.2T Ethernet switches, such as Minipack3 with Dynamic Load Balancing and the NVIDIA Spectrum-4 switch ASIC-based Minipack3N with NVIDIA’s Adaptive Routing on ConnectX NICs. Both DSF and NSF are based on Meta’s FBOSS networking stack, giving us the control to rapidly iterate on and optimize the fabrics in Prometheus, and the visibility to operate these clusters at scale. Aggregation The Backend Aggregation (BAG) network is a multi-layer hub-and-spoke network that connects building-level fabrics across the Prometheus cluster, spanning 2 km to over 100 km. It is built with Arista 7800-series chassis running deep-buffered Broadcom Jericho3 silicon, delivering multiple Pbps of bandwidth per region pair. Running pretraining over this network required a dedicated optimization effort with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure training was not slowed down, especially given speed-of-light constraints at these distances. Pulling this all together, the complexity of the Prometheus network involves millions of miles of fiber strand, tens of thousands of switches, and millions of optics — from 2×400G FR4 LITE short-reach, low-cost pluggables inside the buildings to 800G-ZR coherent optics for links beyond ~10 km. Engineering Reliability at Every Level At Prometheus’ scale, every component needs to be monitored for reliability. A single fault anywhere can halt an entire training job and waste valuable compute resources. Maintaining reliability at this level requires a co-engineering model with NVIDIA that goes beyond a traditional vendor dynamic. Teams are deeply embedded at our data centers, sharing real-time telemetry and running joint triage sessions to decompose every system halt by its root cause. This attribution-driven accountability model ensures both sides are focused on targeted improvements. While Meta optimizes scheduling and infrastructure, NVIDIA addresses firmware, signal diagnostics, and memory handling. This transparency eliminates ambiguity and drives faster fixes across both organizations. The 72-GPU Failure Domain The transition from the H100 generation’s NVL8 architecture to NVL72 has fundamentally redefined our approach to infrastructure resilience. In the NVL8 era, the scale-up domain — the group of GPUs tightly coupled via NVLink for tensor parallelism — was limited to eight units. With NVL72, that domain expands to 72 GPUs, increasing the fault blast radius by 9X. The larger scale-up domain is what gives NVL72 its bandwidth advantage, but it also makes the 72-GPU rack the unit of allocation we plan capacity around. Training parallelism maps most efficiently onto power-of-two group sizes, so each NVL72 domain runs a 64-GPU slice and keeps its remaining eight GPUs as in-rack spares. When a GPU fails, a spare takes its place immediately, so the job restarts from its last checkpoint instead of waiting on hardware repair, and the rack stays in the job. The in-rack redundancy pushes the effective rack fault rate down to the floor set by failures that can remove an entire pod; for rarer whole-rack faults we hold roughly 2% additional racks in reserve. For a 32,768 active-GPU training run, this means provisioning 523 NVL72 racks, or 37,656 GPUs, about 13% above the active footprint. Most of that margin (11%) falls out of the 64-of-72 slice geometry rather than being an absolute reliability tax. Physical complexity further intensifies these reliability requirements. A single NVL72 domain incorporates 5,184 tuned differential-pair signaling links operating at 200 Gbps, each traversing multiple potential points of failure, including GPU SerDes, compute tray PCBs, cable cartridges, and switch tray interfaces. Maintaining consistent signal integrity across this dense fabric — at 200 Gbps per lane — represents an unprecedented engineering challenge at this scale. Fault Recovery Fault recovery addresses how we react to faults to minimize the impact on training time. Depending on the scope (i.e., blast area) of a fault we address it through two mechanisms: Parallelism-Aware Fault Tolerance (PAFT): When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training. The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput. Checkpointing: When a fault blast area is larger than a data-parallel model replica, the entire job is restarted back to the last checkpoint; frequent checkpointing reduces the amount of work lost in these events. Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage. We use delta checkpointing and in-memory staging to ensure these saves happen with minimal impact on training throughput. These two fault recovery mechanisms combine with a sparing strategy that utilizes pre-allocated spare GPU trays within a rack, as well as spare racks, to minimize the time to bring up replacement hardware and reduce the amount of work lost to hardware failures Systematic Reduction of Interruptions When training frontier models, infrastructure reliability requires a perspective beyond simple availability. The fundamental challenge lies in maintaining training momentum without frequent system halts. Within Prometheus, we classify an interruption as any fault — from GPU silicon defects and network fabric anomalies to storage bottlenecks or thermal limits — that forces a job to pause and initiate a recovery cycle. These interruptions introduce a large operational overhead because our workloads are tightly interdependent; a single fault within a 72-GPU domain can affect the entire cluster’s aggregate throughput. This performance loss directly impacts our engineering iteration speed, resulting in less effective compute and longer timelines for delivering advanced AI experiences to billions of people. During the initial phase of Prometheus in mid-2025, our interruption rates reached a peak of nearly 1,000 events per 8K GPUs daily. Through a year of rigorous cross-functional engineering, we have achieved a 99% reduction in interruptions, enabling the cluster to sustain multiple training jobs of tens of thousands of GPUs in parallel. Attaining this stability required a granular decomposition of every interruption source, followed by the deployment of targeted engineering solutions for each failure category: NVLink Signal Integrity: initially the primary bottleneck for GB200 deployments. With over 600,000 NVLink connections, even marginal signal degradation triggers frequent NVLink recovery cycles. We implemented continuous telemetry and automated flagging, utilizing L11 diagnostic burns to isolate weak links before production. Our classification tools distinguish transient faults from persistent signal integrity failures, guiding targeted repairs and component replacement, and we validate repaired systems before returning them to production. Memory Reliability (HBM and LPDDR): Memory-related faults became a major source of interruptions as we scaled GB300 with higher memory capacities. Working closely with NVIDIA, we used fleet telemetry and detailed error analysis to identify recurring failure signatures, which are mitigated via refined HBM firmware settings, memory scrubbing, an improved error correction algorithm for LPDDR, and pattern-based predictive detection to retire degrading devices before they impact job throughput. We are deploying these changes across the fleet and measuring their impact on interruption rates and hardware replacement demand. NVLink Switch and Fabric Health: A single switch fault can compromise an entire NVL72 domain. We monitor fabric health at millisecond resolution, utilizing automated recovery paths to isolate faulty components and rebalance traffic across the remaining infrastructure without a job interruption. Backend Network Events: At the BAG super-spine layer, link events are managed transparently via hardware-based fault detection. Our planar topologies ensure that individual fiber or port failures are rerouted without interrupting the synchronized GPU traffic bursts. Sustained improvement is driven by our operational infrastructure: A colocated triage team at the New Albany site, a comprehensive stability sprint in March that synchronized fixes across the stack, and a rigorous attribution-driven accountability framework. Every repair undergoes a mandatory quarantine to validate system integrity before returning to the compute pool. Our reliability north star remains two interruptions per 8K GPUs per day, which is ~100k GPU hours MTBI. Driving a 99% reduction from our peak interruptions rate demonstrates that, at Prometheus’ scale, stability is an engineering challenge with solvable engineering outcomes. Maturing Hardware at Fleet Scale Deploying hundreds of thousands of first-generation accelerators reveals quality issues that are hidden at lower volumes. The GB200 deployment has transformed hardware maturation into a primary engineering discipline for our teams and partners. Areas of engineering include: Rapid Firmware Bundle Deployment: We built reliable and fast firmware bundle automation, capable of deploying firmware and driver fixes to more than 100k GPUs within a few hours. We’ve brought down the P90 of single-pod upgrade times from more than seven hours in early hardware introduction to two hours. This has let us push rapid fixes for the top interruption categories to our fleet. Fleet Health: We correlate telemetry across multi-rack systems and classify every job interruption to guide software fixes, hardware repairs, and replacement decisions. We track MTBI alongside available capacity plus effective training throughput, and have a robust feedback cycle for hardware and software reliability improvements to translate into more productive compute. Cross-Partner Qualification: implementing parallel validation with multiple manufacturing partners to ensure consistent quality through continuous feedback from our production fleet. Automated Signal Screening: validating over 600,000 NVLink paths using diagnostic stress tests before any production traffic is routed. Even minor defect rates at this scale require proactive identification. Power Delivery Stress Testing: investigating how PSU modules and voltage regulators interact under the 1,400W load of individual GPUs to surface failure modes that only appear at high volumes. Precision Liquid Cooling: enforcing strict quality gates for cold plate and manifold assembly to maintain optimal junction temperatures and prevent leaks across the fleet. Fleet Maintenance: proactive preparation, rapid disposition, prioritization for fix-repair, and prepositioning spares. Health Checks: advanced ingestion/burn-in and pre-job health checks used to identify healthy nodes for inclusion in large training jobs. Each new platform architecture — from Blackwell to Vera Rubin — incorporates these real-world operational insights, tightening our screening and design specifications at every step. Optimizing Power and Managing Transients Maximizing throughput for a given power envelope, minimizing stranded power, and synchronous distributed training introduces a power delivery hurdle. When tens of thousands of GPUs execute compute-heavy phases and communication cycles in unison, they trigger large power transients — sudden load fluctuations of 30-40% within the cluster. Initiating or pausing a major training job can shift loads of more than tens of megawatts in just seconds. We address this with Dynamo Dimmer, our cluster-wide power management framework that enables intelligent power capping. Instead of hard-stopping workloads, Dimmer gradually adjusts GPU power limits as the cluster nears its electrical ceiling, ensuring training continues uninterrupted. This system is reinforced by rack-level battery backup (BBU) modules that handle immediate spikes, capacitor trays (CBUs) for peak smoothing, facility-level battery energy storage systems (BESS), and deep coordination with utility providers to manage these unique AI profiles. Managing Cooling in a Heterogenous Fleet While our distributed approach has allowed us to build Prometheus quickly, it has also meant navigating site-specific power and cooling constraints across different locations. Our physical infrastructure incorporates multiple cooling generations to deliver the liquid cooling required by these high-power racks. Prometheus runs on a mix of modular air-assisted liquid cooling (AALC), including our free-air data center buildings and our rapid-deployment structures. Our purpose-built AI-optimized building now uses facility liquid cooling (FLC) for maximum power density. By integrating leased capacity from strategic partners in addition to our own buildings, we accelerate our deployment timelines and total deployable capacity. Meanwhile, our industrial-grade rapid-deployment structures have redefined the construction playbook, delivering production-ready compute with faster timelines. Operating Efficiently In New Albany, we’ve long partnered with local utilities to ensure we are paying the full cost of energy for our site and not adding any unnecessary strain to the local grid. We’ve also partnered with energy developers to match our energy use with new clean and renewable energy. Meta’s newest AI-optimized data centers use closed-looped, liquid cooling as it is the most efficient way to cool GPU servers, and supports efficient use of water. Direct-to-chip, closed-loop liquid cooling helps save space by allowing us to fit more GPUs on a server rack. We also work to extend our sustainability work by sharing designs for systems like IcePack, our liquid-cooled network rack, with the wider industry through OCP. Beyond Prometheus We’ll continue to work closely with NVIDIA to expand Prometheus’ capacity with a mix of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72s and NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72s. NVIDIA’s next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 platform will be a generational leap in per-GPU performance and will integrate directly into Prometheus’s existing network fabric. As the cluster matures, it will deliver even more compute per watt by augmenting its capacity (primarily interconnected GB300s) with Vera Rubin via our upcoming San Miguel platform. The San Miguel Vera Rubin NVL72 will feature: 72 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs with 288 GB of HBM4 and 19.2 TB/s peak bandwidth per GPU. 2.52 peak EFLOPS of FP4 training compute 1.26 peak EFLOPS FP8 training per rack. 216 TB/s peak NVLink bandwidth (3 TB/s bidirectional per GPU). ~1,500 TB/s peak aggregate memory bandwidth. Fully liquid-cooled compute trays at over 170 kW per rack. 10-20% improvement in performance per watt over the GB300 NVL72. The technological accomplishments within Prometheus have helped establish the blueprint that will inform how we approach the complexity of supercluster design going forward. Hyperion, our upcoming supercluster in Richland Parish, Louisiana, is being designed from the ground up with insights from Prometheus in mind. It will feature closed-loop liquid cooling, full grid connectivity with our utility partner Entergy, for which Meta pays the full cost, and next-generation network designs. Learn more about our community efforts in New Albany. The post Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: Review: Lanterns is a truly unique twist on the superhero genre
items.author: Jennifer Ouellette
items.content: The trailers for HBO's DC Universe series Lanterns teased a show that eschewed the usual superhero hijinks in favor of a gritty realism more in the vein of True Detectives or Slow Horses. Personally, I liked the change. My verdict: Ignore the review bombing; it's wonderful. The season wrapped with an emotionally charged, almost elegaic finale that fully delivered on that initial promise. I've found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives. But Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre. (Spoilers below, but no major reveals.) There are two primary storylines. The first takes place in 2016 with a mass shooting at a local football game in Rushville, Nebraska. Current Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and his new trainee, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), get involved in the investigation, to the annoyance of Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald), who initially doesn't think the case has any extraterrestrial connection. She is soon proved wrong when the suspect (an alien) self-detonates. Hal's power ring controls the damage, but the mystery remains. Read full article Comments

items.title: I Can See Everything
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: Nick Cammarata of Goodfire makes a bold claim: Neural Networks are Already Clean. This was his follow up after various resulting online discussions. This is clearly good work that tells us new and important things. The question is, how big an update is this, how much progress does it represent and what is the outlook going forward? The reactions here range from the super optimistic takes of ‘this means mechanistic interpretability is solvable,’ or even ‘all but solved,’ with comparisons to the famous paper Attention is All You Need. Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): There is so much to say about this, and I will, but WOW, congratulations to Nick and Goodfire. This may be one of the most important single days in deep learning history, and perhaps much more than that. No matter what, this is a victory for the dogged pursuit of understanding. roon (OpenAI): when nick told me that he had some interp breakthroughs, he was uh, underselling it. i think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history. news so good even Eliezer will have to lower his pdoom. we can start making alignment into a ‘normal science’ This paper is solid and meaningful contribution that is in some ways overstated. Get excited, but also there are those who need to take a chill pill. We did not actually get an apples-to-apples jump from 1.7% to 90% interpretability of LLM neurons. I interpret Eliezer as slightly lowering his p(doom), but not all that much. Evžen Wybitul: What’s happening? Half of my tl is non-interp people from OAI painting the post as the second coming of Christ and the other half is interp researchers (including Leo Gao) saying it’s… fine This post is my attempt to sort this out. Currently I am landing somewhere in the middle. It is an important update about how LLMs and minds form and operate. It tells us how to go about some useful tasks and reduces our estimate of some task difficulties. Great work, assuming the work checks out. The whole thing very much has a ring of truth, and of a person being curious. You love to see it. What it does not tell us is that interpretability will soon be solved, or is about to be made into a science, let alone that alignment will soon be handled. The hype got rather out of hand in some places. Table of Contents Good Smoke, Potential Fire. One Neuron, One Central Concept. I Can See Everything. What a Concept. The More You Know. Attention Is Still What You Need. Occam’s Razor. The Neurons Sometimes Share Clear Themes. Hype. Anti-Hype. Theme and Variations. Is This How Minds Work? But We Can Open The Box, Said Toad. That Was Not the Hard Problem. More Skepticism. That’s All There Is, There Ain’t No More. The Default Outcome of Mech Interp is Goodhart’s Law. Interpretability is Dual Use. Now The Work Can Begin. Good Smoke, Potential Fire Before I cover reactions or take a side, here are my highlights. It is worth reading at least this much of the primary source. Reading the whole thing is an option, but it is long and the writing can be easy to bounce off of and can repeat itself. Nick Cammarata, Goodfire: The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought. I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks. After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. One Neuron, One Central Concept The central claim is that for larger LLMs, most neurons represents a singular concept and things clustered around that concept, perhaps with small offshoots and some use of low-level activations. … Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. … With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. Where previously the working theory was that models overloaded neurons with unrelated concepts in superposition, Nick’s theory is you did not think sufficiently hard to identify the unifying concept. Each neuron is a generalization, mostly ones we can readily understand if we look. … What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place. Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. … So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. … Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. … Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. This pictures intelligence as brute force. Neurons are compound words in German. New concept? Go get another neuron. And yet, it works. I Can See Everything … The bad news about modern neural networks is that they’re enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place. In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. Nick argues that this means that it is easier to solve the full puzzle and understand everything, and then take a measurement of your specific area of interest, then to try to directly pull a fuzzy concept like ‘deception’ out of a pool of mystery neurons. … “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. … All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps. Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them. With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect. Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit. Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed. That’s been the pattern for deep learning in general: the simple thing at absurd scale beats the clever one. This claim is maximal and bold, and will get directly challenged. Most people seem to have updated from this paper that more neurons have central singular concepts behind them than we previously thought. Nick is trying to go further, and say that this is what is going on universally. What a Concept … I opened up the cat and car image grid I’d seen hundreds of times before and did something I’d never done: I spent a few seconds wondering what one thing this might be. Almost instantly it was obvious: it’s not a cat and car neuron, it’s a V-shape neuron. there are Lady Reds in the future: What is this extremely mysterious neuron that set mechinterp going on a dead end for the last 3 years? It’s literally </\> kiki ? or bouba o0o Remember this the next time you think you can never figure anything out, or that surely people have already asked the basic questions and considered the obvious. Maybe they have. Maybe they haven’t. Paper (resuming): … InceptionV1 has more than a hundred of these generalized pose neurons, each one its own clean detector of a pose shared across cars, dogs and other objects, and to my knowledge no one had noticed them. … I can often unblock my understanding of a neuron by asking: if I couldn’t use groups of nouns at all, how would I describe this neuron to someone else? … We should treat a neuron that means two or three things as one neuron with a few grouped meanings. The grouping probably wasn’t a problem for the network: the meanings sit together because, from the network’s point of view, they’re similar. … Polysemanticity is often more a claim about the observer than the neuron. It says there’s no good explanation yet. There’s a few reasons that could be: Bad tools: our lens or microscope isn’t good enough Bad explanations: created from those tools Bad learning: the network learned poorly due to bad architecture, training data, or something else Recursive generalization: while generalizing, the neuron branched off in a few related directions Superposition: a change in learning principle where the network packs unrelated things into the same neurons because they rarely collide. … In a frontier language model, I found a neuron that mostly fired on “pr”, but also on a bunch of Base64 URL strings as well as some Bengali. I thought this must finally be an arbitrary mixture. But decode the URLs: “pr” words. Translate the Bengali: “pr”. … In a dense Qwen model, a coworker came across a neuron that standard top-k automated interpretability lists as a “polysemantic comma neuron”. But looking more closely, it turned out to track Colorado: phone numbers, slang, and connections to other Colorado neurons. Steering it made the model want to go hiking. The commas were where it stored a running summary of the Colorado context so far. In general attention seems to collect on the punctuation, which we call the summary motif. Once you know it, a lot of similar neurons get easier to understand. … In another case a neuron looked like an arbitrary mess, with nothing firing strongly. It turns out it looked for specific signs within pages of health SEO spam, and once we had a sufficiently broad dataset, it was understandable. Nick does notice the skulls that result from going full ‘This Is Not a Coincidence Because Nothing Is Ever a Coincidence.’ … This risks the opposite error, an explanation of the gaps: assuming every neuron must have a sensible story. Two things make it less worrying. First, each of the other causes can be tested. … Second, real explanations tend to be narrow and easily testable. Once you suspect a neuron is a Colorado neuron, steer it and see what it says. The strong hypothesis is that neurons will all have central concepts like Colorado. The even stronger hypothesis is that there will not also be unrelated additional concepts happening behind the scenes. … I used to think of neurons as human-shaped nouns: one is a car, another is a curve. Now I think of them more as control flow. A neuron is less about what it sees than about what it does to the flow coming in, and often its job is to gate a region of the network. … The negative side of neurons matters almost as much as positives for understanding them, even in ReLU networks where the negative side is cut off. … Some neurons hold their meaning far down the range; others drop off a cliff, like the Christmas neuron above at about 5% of its max. Some fire a few times a book, others a few times a page. The More You Know The core theory is that perhaps intelligence is a simpler concept than we think? It is all a series of coherent concepts with links? There’s a ‘Hitchhiker’s Guide state unit that peaks on the title and the Answer slot’ that weakly fires on all 42s? There is a neuron specifically for the joke about fusion always being a fixed amount into the future that fires on other similar repeated promises? What we see is about 90% of neurons having basically one job, with recursive generalization offshoots that are usually related. … I’ve never seen a neuron with something like ten unrelated things it does. Nick Cammarata, Goodfire: Here’s an attribution graph from Kimi K3 using only neurons. As far as we know, it’s the first published attribution graph of a multiple trillion parameter model. Asked what to do with a wallet it found, it links the wallet, the cash and the owner’s ID to lost property and honesty, and answers “return”. We haven’t begun full audits of this scale yet, and hope to soon, but so far most things have been intuitively interpretable. Simple things done well. Echoes. Vibes. No papers or essays, only references to papers and essays. A fully bitter lesson. The more bitter, the easier the lesson.
