Similarly, my impression is that SAEs generally don’t find things that are a single neuron, or even very sparse in the neuron basis, and are often a better basis for certain tasks than the neuron basis, though the evidence base is kinda weak here since we largely focus on residual stream or layer output SAEs, I’d love to see work on this in Goodfire’s forthcoming paper! I also think residual stream SAEs are extremely useful, as they give a good bottleneck of the model’s information at this token and layer, and I don’t see a good way to replicate them in the neuron framework. And kudos to Nick for updating a bunch of his historical vision work! Revisiting old results with modern tools and more rigour seems great. Nick responded directly, including claiming weak activations are ‘surprisingly ablateable,’ and they went back and forth. You also can and should start out skeptical on priors. Most hyped results are hyped. Samuel Albanie (Google DeepMind): on base rates, I’m a little skeptical of big positive updates on mech interp. On the other hand, orders of magnitude more ai labour will be coming online in the near future, so the Hamming adage applies: “In almost all fields, a factor of ten means fundamentally new effects. If you increase magnification by a factor of 10 in Biology, you will see new things.” so it doesn’t seem implausible that scaling the simple approach will work. will be watching closely. The bull case is a combination of ‘we could not do this at scale before and now we can’ with ‘it turns out the neurons mostly have singular explanations, so we can do it at all,’ bitter lesson, go. Seems plausible, so long as you do not get overexcited. That’s All There Is, There Ain’t No More If minds are largely neurons representing specific central concepts, that then have associations with other concepts in these atomic fashions, one might ask ‘is that all?’ Zvi Mowshowitz: Still reading through this and processing. I’m less struck by the ‘now we can do interpretability easier’ part – you still have to understand what you see – and more by the ‘so you are saying this is all there is to intelligence?’ part. That’s it? Elijah Ravitz-Campbell: I feel like this very much matches how I imagined AI might work before I knew anything about it in practice. A sort of hand wavy “you know concepts have nodes and relationships between those nodes in code semantic knowledge”. roon: Yeah I’m surprised so few are grappling with the philosophical implications of all this antra: I don’t think that’s it, and I think this is kind of why SD is a lot more interpretable than transformers. This applies to some degree to parts of perceptive, semantic and motoric representations of language models, but not as much to compositional, integrative and temporal ones. I am also quite sus of weak activation dismissal on strongly recurrent networks like transformers. We saw weak activations matter strongly specifically in the temporal/recureent domain, which is ignored by this paper. Does this mean that perhaps a dumber mind can understand a smarter one, if all the components are understandable, the same way we can understand complex biological systems, or the components of complex systems or organizations? Certainly you can ‘understand’ something that has advantages over you. If the AI is faster than you, or can memorize more things, it is easy to see how you can understand and even predict it. If intelligence were sufficiently a pure ‘more simple things combined’ in some sense, then you might have a shot when moving at slow speed? That likely presumes that the ‘real action’ is in the neurons, or other places we can parse. We should not assume that. Can we even simulate a neuron? Leo Gao (OpenAI): this is cool work, but i think people are overupdating on how optimistic to be about interp. in particular, we need to more rigorously evaluate explanations, rather than just going off vibes. imo if you can’t simulate a neuron you haven’t really explained it. my guess is simulating the neurons is way harder than finding plausible explanations. I have a post on this in the works. (i know the blog talks argues simulations are bad, but i think all of the downsides described are avoided by looking at KL instead of neuron correlation.) Nick: would love to read it when it’s ready. I haven’t thought enough about simulation scores to be super confident, and could somewhat easily be convinced back My understanding is that previously we only found ~1.7% of neurons interpretable back in 2023 (Bills et al) but that the test for this required predicting activations. Nick is not yet trying to predict activations. The Default Outcome of Mech Interp is Goodhart’s Law What happens if we apply optimization pressure to which neurons light up? Depending on strong or direct the optimization pressure gets, that could be The Most Forbidden Technique. An AI produces a final output [X] via some method [M]. You can analyze [M] using technique [T], to learn what the AI is up to. You could train on that. Never do that. You train on [X]. Only [X]. Never [M], never [T]. Why? Because [T] is how you figure out when the model is misbehaving. If you train on [T], you are training the AI to obfuscate its thinking, and defeat [T]. You will rapidly lose your ability to know what is going on, in exactly the ways you most need to know what is going on. Those bits of optimization pressure from [T] are precious. Use them wisely. We must continue to never, ever train on the interpretability, and to watch out for other indirect ways we are doing so. There will be crazy amounts of pressure to pull out forms of The Most Forbidden Technique. Simon Lermen: Fundamentally, trying to automate alignment research points an objective at “convince the human” for the AI to optimize for. If this plan was to be taken even a little serious you’d expect the AI labs to have very seriously thought about solid metrics and benchmarks that aren’t just going to get goodhearted immediately. Instead we will likely see a last-minute vibe-coded “alignment solution” born from the lethal arrogance of the AI lunatics. I don’t think this is ‘lethal arrogance of the AI lunatics.’ I think it is that the AI creators are doing the best they can given that they are under extreme time pressure, so everything is always last-minute vibe coded. Once you vibe code it then that becomes the last minute. My baseline scenario is that the labs will not do the maximally stupid direct optimization thing, but that some others will, and that the labs will end up doing a bunch of indirect optimizations that exert pressure. How much damage results from that pressure will remain unclear. One way I would expect AIs to adapt to this pressure is to learn how to think about [X] without triggering the direct neurons or detectors for [X]. Do not rely on your detectors in ways that presume future AIs won’t learn to get around them. We already see places the AI could hide such thinking. There are 2%-5% of unexplained polls, and weak activations look like they could be cheaply ablated and thus are available for other things, plus we don’t understand the cache or attention. Interpretability is Dual Use One must also remember that essentially everything in alignment is dual use. Roon: pretraining science is kind of like how people built quite good steam engines before they understood thermodynamics. “Science owes more to the steam engine than the steam engine owes to science.”-(L.J. Henderson). if nick is right, which i am pretty sure he is, progress points in the direction of more interpretability, and pretraining was “slouching towards monosemanticity”. my guess would be that major breakthroughs in interp also advance capabilities Nathan: If ‘positive’ updates like this are, as roon says, likely to increase capabilities, then funding safety work has an unclear effect on safety. Interpretability is even more dual use than usual. I still strongly support working on it, but very obviously if you can figure out what the neurons do, or better yet how the whole operation works and thinks, you can use that to increase capabilities. A lot of my first thoughts were how to use this information to improve training, which could then be spent on any combination of seeking alignment or seeking other things. Now The Work Can Begin What does this all add up to? Partly that will boil down to how much of this holds up. We have not yet seen the technical paper. I think this news represents a substantial update in the difficulty of neuron interpretability, and in the ways in which LLMs organize their information and thoughts. This should make it much easier to attack interpretability through a neuron analysis lens than previously thought, and open up a lot of good research and understanding. I do not think this mean interpretability, let alone alignment, is on its way to being solved. We should be pessimistic about how far such claimed breakthroughs go, the same way SAEs are useful but not as useful as some hoped. Even if they are fully real and work out about maximally well, this is the beginning of the work, not the end, and many things are missing. We still need to know what is up with weak activations, with the cache and with attention. We still will have little idea how the AIs are thinking, or why they are able to do the breakthroughs and impressive feats. We will not have any guarantee that, if in a hostile situation, our techniques would hold, especially against future AIs, even before we apply optimization pressure over time. We also need to worry the result largely will not hold up. The Colorado-Tornado result suggests that the whole thing might be a lot less clean than it appears. I updated a substantial negative amount from the eagerness to jump on the hype train. It pattern matched quite a lot with ‘we will once again pretend we will have everything handled and therefore only invest in these prosaic plans right until we run into another wall and realize this is insufficient.’ We need to fight hard against that. This is still excellent news. The world is more hopeful now. Let’s get to work.

items.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
items.author: BrianKrebs
items.content: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom. Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year. In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization. The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI. Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts. According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States. Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out). On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal. A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach. That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files. SHINYWIRE KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates. A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website. The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands. The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email. The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials. Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor). In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive. The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.” Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder. GHOSTBYTE According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid. A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com. “If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.” An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok. It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account. Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019). In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media. “We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.” The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner. CONFLICTING INTERESTS It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government. Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms. In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack). But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records. A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on. The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice. The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates. The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business. “Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.” In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story. “I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned. The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group. Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid. That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price. “It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.” Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions. “There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said. In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million. In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

items.title: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents
items.author: Emma Roth
items.content: A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge. Though Norforge doesn't name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins. Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time, rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks of their own after escaping from testing environments. Researchers at Norforge uncovered the attacks through exposed work on Cai … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.title: It’s hard to imagine wireless headphones ever getting lighter than these
items.author: Andrew Liszewski
items.content: If you're on the hunt for lightweight wireless headphones but wearing earbuds or clip-ons never feels comfortable or secure, a relatively obscure Japanese headphone maker could have the solution. Final's new Porta headphones feature an on-ear design supported by a headband but with a structure made from a single piece of wire so they weigh just 40 grams. For comparison, Marshall's recently-launched Milton A.N.C. are also designed to be smaller on-ear headphones but weigh 200 grams. The Final Porta are available for preorder now through the company's online store for 12,800 yen (around $80) with black or orange ear pads and shipping expected … Read the full story at The Verge.

items.title: Elon Musk promises to give one SpaceX share to every child in the US
items.author: Emma Roth
items.content: Elon Musk says he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in the US starting next year. With around 72 million children in the US as of July 2025, Musk would be giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, according to a report from CNBC. Musk, who runs SpaceX and Tesla, writes on X that this giveaway "will be the first of many." It comes just months after SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell announced that she'd be giving shares of her SpaceX stock to 2 million Trump Accounts, the tax-advantaged investment accounts given to American children. Dell's founder similarly poured $6.25 billion into Trump Accounts, while Micron also … Read the full story at The Verge.
