items.title: AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Lambda Web Functions, Amazon S3 on the Vercel Marketplace, and more (October 19, 2026)
items.author: Daniel Abib
items.content: Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction. The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines AWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code. Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control. The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel – You can now provision S3 general purpose buckets, S3 Tables, and S3 Vectors from the Vercel dashboard, or by describing what you want to build in v0. It joins existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, so the whole stack sits in one AWS account with one bill. The authentication detail is the good part: a short-lived OIDC token is exchanged at runtime with AWS Security Token Service for credentials scoped to that resource, so no static keys are stored anywhere. Amazon EC2 T8i instances are now available in South America (São Paulo) – The newest burstable generation reached the São Paulo Region, which matters for the unglamorous half of a workload: login gateways, small databases, CI/CD runners, low-traffic sites. Amazon EC2 T8i delivers up to 30 percent better price performance than T3, with up to 70 percent higher compute performance and 2.4 times the Amazon EBS bandwidth. It keeps the same CPU credit system as T3, so moving over is a size change rather than a redesign, and t8i.micro and t8i.small are available under the AWS Free Tier. Reflection Beam, an open-weight model for agentic coding, is now on AWS – You can now deploy Beam, Reflection AI’s open-weight model for agentic coding and long-horizon tasks, from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. It’s a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 501 billion total and 23 billion active parameters, released on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0, and Reflection reports an effective context length of 1 million tokens. Start with a JumpStart real-time endpoint, or use SageMaker HyperPod Inference with SGLang or vLLM when you need Kubernetes-native control. It was also ported and optimized for AWS Trainium3, and launches in N. Virginia and Ohio. AWS Lambda Durable Execution SDK for Go is now generally available – You can now write multi-step Go workflows that checkpoint their own progress and pause for up to a year while waiting on an external event, without building progress tracking yourself. That covers deployment rollouts with approval gates and pipelines that call a model and then stop for human review. It behaves like ordinary Go tooling: go get to add it, deploy a single static binary on the provided.al2023 runtime, and test a full workflow locally with the durabletest package, no network access or credentials required. Amazon CloudWatch announces log routing and chained log parsers – You can now define routes in an Amazon CloudWatch pipeline that send each event to a different log group based on conditions evaluated against processed fields, so severity, source, or event type can each land somewhere with its own retention and access controls. Chained parsers handle the other half: parsers run in sequence, with later ones consuming fields that earlier ones produced, so you can parse a JSON envelope first and then run a Grok parser over a field it extracted. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: AWS Security Agent exploited 33 of 37 new real-world CVEs – The team pointed their autonomous penetration-testing agent, now part of AWS Continuum, at 37 recently disclosed CVEs packaged as live containerized targets, starting from nothing but an endpoint URL and a one-line hint. It captured 35 flags, and after auditing every win against the challenge’s canonical proof of concept, 33 of 37 (89.2 percent) held up as genuine end-to-end exploitation. The two misses are what make the post worth your time: in both, the agent found and exploited the bug, then took the target down before it could read the flag. A capable autonomous attacker is also a destructive one. Your serverless attendee’s guide to AWS re:Invent 2026 – A curated path through a very large catalog, worth having before the good sessions fill up. How Dynata scaled AI across the development lifecycle with AI-DLC and Kiro IDE – What changes when agentic coding stops being an individual habit and becomes how a team works. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. Here in Brazil, the 2026 season closes with AWS Community Day Brasil Norte in Belém on October 31, the final stop in a year that covered every region of the country for the first time. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! — Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

items.title: EFF Launches Privacy Badger for Safari on macOS
items.author: Hudson Hongo
items.content: Free Tracker Blocker Used by Millions Will Protect Even More Users' Privacy SAN FRANCISCO—Privacy Badger, the award-winning tracker blocker made by the member-supported digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), is now available for Safari on macOS. Safari users can download the free browser extension today and join the more than 4 million people using Privacy Badger to take a stand against data brokers and online surveillance. Users will need Safari version 26.5 or higher to use it. Ranked as one of the best ad tracker blockers by The Wirecutter, Consumer Reports, PC Mag and more, Privacy Badger is different from other blocking extensions. Created by EFF to stop companies from spying on you online, Privacy Badger automatically learns to block hidden trackers on the web, along with additional privacy-protecting features. "Most websites contain invisible tracking code that lets companies collect, share, and profit from your personal data," said Lena Cohen, Staff Technologist at EFF. "Creepy ads are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the harms of online tracking: Once your information enters the data broker ecosystem, it’s nearly impossible to know who buys it or what they’re doing with it. Safari support has long been one of Privacy Badger’s most requested features and EFF is excited to be able to make this important tool available to Safari users to fight back for a better web." On Safari, Privacy Badger goes beyond the browser’s built-in privacy features to provide additional protection against online tracking. In its default browsing mode, Safari limits the information that trackers can access, but it still allows them to load. Privacy Badger blocks online trackers from loading in the first place, preventing them from tracking you using techniques that bypass Safari’s protections. With today's launch, Privacy Badger is now available on all major desktop browsers. As the leading nonprofit defending online civil liberties, EFF is committed to fighting mass surveillance in the courts, through activism, and by making free, privacy-protecting tools like Privacy Badger. Now, even more people can join the movement against online tracking, by installing Privacy Badger themselves, telling their friends and family who use Safari about it, or by supporting Privacy Badger today. For more on Privacy Badger for Safari on macOS: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2026/10/announcing-privacy-badger-safari-macos For more on the dangers of online tracking: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/03/online-tracking-out-control-privacy-badger-can-help-you-fight-back For more on how Privacy Badger works: https://privacybadger.org/ Contact: press@eff.org Tags: Privacy Badger Ad trackers Surveillance Advertising

items.title: GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary
items.content: Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world knowledge built into LLMs makes ad matching more intelligent and precise, compounding gains for advertisers. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Rather than maintaining a dedicated ID for every item, GenRecs Tokenization represents each item with a set of tokens from a stable semantic vocabulary. Paired with Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) and Meta’s Adaptive Ranking Model, GenRecs Tokenization has delivered a +0.35% lift in conversions across surfaces for advertisers. GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders, GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal. GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases: Accelerating learning from new entities: Semantic tokenization helps models to infer relevance and establish relationships through shared concepts. New entities include newly created ads, niche products, and pages with limited engagement. Enabling cross-campaign transfer: Semantic tokenization creates a stable vocabulary that allows the models to carry insights across campaigns for advertisers. LLM scaling benefits: Semantic tokenization allows the benefits to compound with the LLM scaling curve’s improving performance. Infusing world knowledge: Semantic tokenization gives pre-trained language models a direct interface to reason about ad content and user intent. Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields: Prediction accuracy improvements in production: Paired with Meta’s GEM and Adaptive Ranking Model, GenRecs Tokenization delivered a +0.35% lift1 in conversions. Compounding feedback loop: Better tail predictions yield better lessons from tail ads which enrich the training data to further improve predictions for all ads from the model, creating a performance improving feedback loop. A new way to scale: Across production ranking and retrieval, tokens bend the scaling curve along sequence length, training data, and model architecture. 1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026. Introducing GenRecs Tokenization Pre-trained multimodal models read each ad, product, and page, including its text and images, and encode the items into an embedding that carries world knowledge. The tokenizer combines that content signal with representations learned from how people engage with the items, then quantizes the result into a short sequence of discrete tokens. Similar items share tokens, much as related words share roots. For example, there’s overlap between two running shoe ads from the previous season to the current season, so the new campaign immediately benefits from everything the model has already learned about the previous season’s products. At the heart of GenRecs Tokenization is a three-stage pipeline that: Encodes each item into a semantic embedding space. Decomposes that embedding into independent subspaces. Quantizes by mapping each subspace to an entry in a codebook. Maximizing ads recommendation quality requires diverse combinations of these stages depending on entity and feature semantics. For example, for many ad representations, GenRecs Tokenization uses prefix n-grams that combine a learned encoder, residual decomposition, learned vector codebooks, and token parametrization. Token Quality Predicts Ranking Accuracy Independently of downstream ranking gain, tokenizer model quality can be evaluated against intrinsic measures like: Cluster purity: The items that share a code tend to share a category, giving the model a cleaner signal per token; Distribution balance: Items spread evenly across semantic IDs instead of crowding into a few. Codebook utilization: A larger share of codes holds at least one item, so the vocabulary expresses more distinctions. Across the eight tokenizer versions we tested, we see a strong correlation between these intrinsic quality metrics and downstream ranking prediction accuracy. Tokenizer versions that scored better on these metrics also had better CTR prediction accuracy for ads models. The Tokenization Flywheel Tokenization maximizes the efficiency of high-volume campaigns by uncovering deeper semantic patterns across their vast product catalogs. For tail ads that accumulate fewer impressions, tokenization enables ads recommendation models to generalize across them via shared content structure, recovering cold-start performance and enabling cross-entity transfer. When a sportswear brand launches next season’s trail shoe, tokenization lets the new product and its ads build on what the model learned from last season’s shoe, even before anyone sees the new ad. By improving tail ad prediction quality, tokenization not only lets tail ads be ranked accurately, but also improves the training data, which then improves prediction quality for all ads. Each pass through this self-reinforcing flywheel improves the quality of model predictions. The Foundations of LLM Recommendation Tokenizer improvements are not confined to the model they were tuned for. Optimizing codebook quality through diversity loss, dead code resets, and contrastive objectives produces measurably better downstream performance when the resulting tokens train generative recommenders. Our work on LLM-native retrieval shows how far this can go. A two-tower architecture built on a shared LLM encoder reaches state-of-the-art retrieval quality while remaining efficiently servable, matching classic two-tower performance on a fraction of the training data. Building on this, we are now extending reasoning-aware ranking on top of the same vocabulary. The Future of GenRecs Tokenization We are continuing to push GenRecs Tokenization toward the ROI-optimal frontier along three directions: Deepening cold-start generalization: Tail ad inventory is where semantic tokens contribute most and where advertiser impact is largest. We are scaling the coverage of tokenization across all items to deliver better performance to advertisers. Treating tokenizer quality as a first-class objective: Engagement-aligned training, unified cross-entity vocabulary, and codebook improvements are active areas of investment. Because intrinsic quality measures predict downstream ranking gains, we can iterate on the tokenizer without waiting on a full model training cycle. Serving LLM-native architectures efficiently: Fully verbalized tokenization gives a model the richest view of an ad, but requires context windows that are impractical at ads scale. We are combining compacted verbalized tokens with semantic IDs to retain reasoning quality while maintaining acceptable latency. Looking further out, we are exploring whether the same vocabulary that improves ads ranking today could unify representation across surfaces. A shared token space spanning ads content across text, image, audio, and video, would let models reason about what a person is interested in and what an advertiser has to offer with one representation, rather than stitching together separately learned embeddings. As recommendation systems evolve from discriminative scoring to include generative reasoning, the data foundation benefits from evolving from ephemeral IDs to stable semantic representations. GenRecs Tokenization provides the foundation, translating the complexity of Meta’s ads ecosystem into a vocabulary that generative models can learn, reason about, and generate from. Acknowledgements We would like to thank Weifeng Cui, Ling Leng, Luke Simon, Hadar Ohana, Jimmy Chen, Minghai Chen, Chiyu Zhang, Dinesh Ramasamy, Debajyoti Roy, Shawn Shi, Gajanan Golegaonkar, Xiao Yang, Ashkan Aleali, Anuj Gargava, Xizhou Feng, Liquan Huang, Frank Shyu, Xiaoyu Chen, Kungang Li, Chonglin Sun, Matt Steiner, Sandeep Pandey, Santanu Kolay, Anuj Madan, Tak Yan, and the entire team behind the development and productionization of the first large scale semantic tokenization effort in Meta’s ad recommendation system. The post GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary appeared first on Engineering at Meta.

items.title: Florida DMV hacked after police dept insecurely stored login info
items.author: Ashley Belanger
items.content: The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) has begun notifying victims impacted by a recent data breach of driver’s license and motor vehicle data, but not everyone whose information was stolen will receive an alert. In a notice posted Friday, FLHSMV confirmed that it took “immediate steps” after discovering that “a malicious actor accessed certain department records on September 4, 2026, using compromised credentials.” There’s “no evidence” that data has yet been misused, the department said, but law enforcement “determined the information potentially affected includes driver license and motor vehicle data, to include document images, and other personal information.” FLHSMV is sending out letters to everyone affected, offering victims one year of credit monitoring from Sontiq, Inc. However, the state acknowledged that it may not have current contact information for many former Florida residents whose data was still being stored. Those potential victims can confirm if their data was stolen by emailing FLHSMV at customerinquiry@flhsmv.gov, officials said. Read full article Comments

items.title: AI game clones are making indie developers afraid to show their work
items.author: Kyle Orland
items.content: Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games, with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms. Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely. Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflex, which had been set to go live with today's launch of Steam Next Fest. In a post on social media Friday evening, the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, "we're concerned that the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch." Read full article Comments

items.title: Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models
items.author: Alex Reneau
items.content: Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic.We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs. Context When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow, a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows. We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models. Introducing System One extraction models Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it. Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds. An extraction model can return: Extracted values: Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score. Including, computed values: Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score. Estimated values: Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval. Forecasted values: Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval. And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look. Here’s how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models: System One: Extract System One: Decide System Two Example models Clairic Jev, Clef GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek Sampling One parallel pass One parallel pass One token at a time Purpose Predict values Make decisions Write and reason ML framing Regression and extraction Classification Generation Thinking mode System 1: fast, one pass System 1: fast, one pass System 2: slow, deliberate Output Typed values: spans, numbers, dates, times, lists, distributions, with calibrated probabilities Typed decisions: options with calibrated probabilities Free-form strings Output space Continuous, but typed and bounded by your schema A finite set of options you list Anything What it answers What's the amount? When does it happen? How much will it be? Which category is it? Is it legitimate? Which action should we take? Why did it happen? How should we approach it? Can you fix it? Output always a valid response? Yes: every answer is a value of its declared type (or null), inside your bounds Yes: answers are always one of your options No: strings must be parsed and checked Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words. How a request works Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurate than an LLM for certain use cases. A request is a state (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed fields. You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language instructions, and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel pass. There is no reasoning and no output tokens – everything computes in a single forward pass, which means it is both fast and cheap. Type Returns text A specific span of the input, with its offsets number A number read or computed, honoring integer and decimals date, time, datetime Calendar dates and valid times, in ISO form duration A length of time in the unit you choose list Matching text, number or date, in input order estimate A distribution inside your [min, max], on your step grid, linear or log scale. forecast One estimate per future step of a series Every scalar answer comes with p_null (the probability that the value isn’t in the inputs) and confidence. Every estimate answer comes with a median and an 80% interval (p10 to p90), plus all 99 percentiles on request. There's no limit on the number of fields: if they don't fit beside the input in one pass, the server splits them into parallel passes that each see the whole input, then merges the answers. Here are some examples to illustrate the model’s features. Of course, using these features in a workflow would require appropriate inputs. An example: Extracting values Extraction is probably the most common job handed to LLMs today: "return the invoice number, vendor and due date as JSON." It works most of the time, but the failure modes are hard to catch. The output may not be valid JSON, a digit can be misread as it's generated, and once a text excerpt comes back, there's no way to trace it to where it appeared in the source. Most people build extraction pipelines to combat this, with multiple layers of parsing, schema validation, retries and spot checks. On top of that, you pay for reasoning and output tokens on every field of every document. Clairic operates differently; it doesn’t generate text answers. Instead, you get: Values extracted from your input, so an answer is grounded. Computed values, so it can parse through unstructured data without pre-sanitizing it. Character offset spans, so you can reference where in the input the data was. Confidence labels, so you can determine which values need a second look. A strongly typed output, so numbers and dates are formed under the rules of their type (e.g., a cents field has two decimals). Handling for null values, where a missing field returns with null as an answer (along with an estimated probability of null and a guess). Cheaper and faster answers, because every field is answered in the same parallel pass. So asking for thirty fields costs about the same as asking for three. Let’s walk through an example to illustrate the ways Clairic can extract values from unstructured data and make estimates. Take a customer support email: Hi, order A-88412 arrived on Sept 28, 2026 with a cracked screen and a dented corner. I paid $649.00 plus $52.10 tax. It's now Oct 9, 2026 and I'd like this fixed or refunded. Thanks, Dana From a Worker, you would make a request to Clairic to process this data: const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", { state: email, fields: { order_id: { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" }, delivered_on: { type: "date", instructions: "Delivery date" }, amount_paid: { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" }, days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true, instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" }, damage: { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" }, tracking_number: { type: "text" }, }, }); Clairic returns the extracted values, spans in the input, probability that it is null (p_null) and confidence score: { "order_id": { "type": "text", "p_null": 3.4e-6, "span": [10, 17], "guess": "A-88412", "confidence": 0.999957, "value": "A-88412" }, "delivered_on": { "type": "date", "p_null": 6.5e-8, "guess": "2026-09-28", "confidence": 0.999999, "value": "2026-09-28" }, "amount_paid": { "type": "number", "p_null": 1.6e-5, "guess": 701.1, "confidence": 0.999944, "value": 701.1 }, "days_since_delivery": { "type": "duration", "p_null": 6.1e-9, "unit": "days", "guess": 11, "confidence": 0.999999, "value": 11 }, "damage": { "type": "list", "value": ["cracked screen", "dented corner"], "spans": [[50, 64], [71, 84]] }, "tracking_number": { "type": "text", "p_null": 1, "span": [106, 112], "guess": "$52.10", "confidence": 0.416016, "value": null } } A few things to notice: amount_paid isn't written anywhere in the email. In this example, Clairic added the price and the tax in the same pass and returns the sum. days_since_delivery is also worked out from two dates in the text, not directly in the input. damage lists both kinds of damage as exact spans, so you can highlight them in the source. tracking_number isn't in the email, so it comes back null instead of a plausible-looking guess. guess shows what the model would otherwise have picked. Clairic also works with images Here’s a real-life photo of a receipt — the text is not perfect and the angle of the image doesn’t help its legibility. We passed this image to Clairic to see what it could extract: { "model": "clairic", "answers": { "order_number": { "type": "number", "p_null": 0.0040206750854849815, "guess": 77245, "confidence": 0.776249383996532, "value": 77245 }, "purchased_at": { "type": "datetime", "p_null": 4.136094133855295e-08, "guess": "2026-07-01T13:34:00", "confidence": 0.831464227002992, "value": "2026-07-01T13:34:00" }, "quantity": { "type": "number", "p_null": 5.2313655629632194e-08, "guess": 2, "confidence": 0.9997007500403496, "value": 2 }, "unit_price": { "type": "number", "p_null": 0.001599092734977603, "guess": 7.99, "confidence": 0.9991279019989127, "value": 7.99 }, "subtotal": { "type": "number", "p_null": 9.69956488461321e-08, "guess": 15.98, "confidence": 0.9999881983893096, "value": 15.98 }, "sales_tax": { "type": "number", "p_null": 2.5511653802823275e-06, "guess": 0, "confidence": 0.9999800924450729, "value": 0 }, "tip": { "type": "number", "p_null": 5.953857908025384e-05, "guess": 2.39, "confidence": 0.9335768781214697, "value": 2.39 }, "discount": { "type": "number", "p_null": 0.9994148015975952, "guess": 0, "confidence": 0.91852733929319, "value": null } } } As you can see, it was able to extract all the values from the images, alongside a confidence score. It also correctly stated that there was no discount shown in the receipt, giving the value as null. An example: Estimating values Some values aren't in the input at all, but the input carries evidence for them. For example, values might not be in plain text but can be discerned from values around it. If you ask an LLM for an estimation, you usually get a single number with no sense of how sure the model is. It will make safe guesses or hallucinate, or reason its way around the answer. If you land on an estimate, any downstream processing can't tell a confident $180 from an unconfident $180, so it can't help you decide what is appropriate to automate in the circumstances. It is also a lot slower and more expensive to do reasoning through LLMs. A decision model can approximate an estimate by choosing among buckets ("under $100", "$100–500", …), but buckets are coarse, every bucket adds input tokens, and each new category adds more sources of confusion for the model during its decision making process. Clairic returns a distribution over the range you declare: a point value, a median, an 80% interval, and every percentile on request. The estimate is designed to fall inside your bounds, so there's nothing to clamp or round afterward. The width of the interval reflects data confidence: a narrow range signals high certainty, while a wide range indicates low certainty, information you can use to route another check. Here’s another example, where Clairic looks at historical home prices and comparable sales, to determine an estimate : const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", { state: `Comparable sales: sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood,sale_price 1450,3,1998,Elm Park,412000 2100,4,2006,Elm Park,585000 980,2,1975,Riverside,265000 1600,3,2003,Elm Park,449000 1300,3,1990,Riverside,318000 Subject property: sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood 1620,3,2001,Elm Park`, fields: { sale_price: { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 50000, max: 5000000, scale: "log", step: 1000 } }); Clairic will return an estimated value: { "sale_price": { "type": "estimate", "value": 418000, "median": 415000, "p10": 370000, "p90": 470000, "p_below": 0.0, "p_above": 0.0 } } Values always fall inside your bounds, and the width of the interval shows how much the input informs the prediction: price is narrow ($370,000-$470,000), days on market is wide (24-148). Because fields are unlimited and answered in parallel, you can score many items in one call (one estimate per candidate, lead, or listing) and sort them in code. An example: Forecasting values Forecasting values in a time series is quite hard for generalized models — it usually means you have to either build a specific pipeline per metric (parse the data, fit a model, tune it, deploy it), or you paste 36 months of numbers into an LLM and ask for the next three. The first is accurate but really expensive and time-consuming to set up for every new series. The second is easy, but you get point forecasts with no intervals, forecasts that shift depending on how the prompt is worded, and answers with limited confidence. Clairic sits between the two — it is not claiming to replace a dedicated time-series model, but it is a little faster and cheaper than your regular LLM. A forecast field takes the history as plain text in state and returns, for every step ahead, a value and an 80% interval, inside the bounds you declare. It reads the history the way you already have it, whether that's a CSV export, a pasted dashboard, or rows mixed with notes, and may often work with no need to clean up your data beforehand. To see how that holds up on real data, we used a public series: the number of people the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screens at U.S. airport checkpoints each day. Each morning we asked Clairic for the next day's count, given the real counts so far, for 21 days in a row: const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", { state: `Daily number of people screened at TSA checkpoints at US airports. date,weekday,travelers 2026-07-16,Thu,2850229 ... 2026-10-13,Tue,2353356 Forecast date: 2026-10-14 (Wed)`, fields: { travelers: { type: "forecast", horizon: 1, interval: "day", min: 500000, max: 4000000, scale: "log", instructions: "Number of people screened tomorrow" }, }, }); Which returns: { "travelers": { "type": "forecast", "value": [2416117], "median": [2419283], "p10": [2270774], "p90": [2556769] } } In actuality, TSA screened 2,419,474 people that day, which is right around the median 2,419,283 that Clairic predicted. Data: TSA checkpoint travel numbers, accessed Oct. 15, 2026. Across the 21 days, Clairic's forecasts were off by 3.3% on average, and 17 of the 21 actual counts landed inside its 80% interval, which follows what an 80% interval should do. It picked up the weekly rhythm from the numbers alone: quieter Tuesdays and Saturdays, busier Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays. The misses are also interesting: three of the four days outside the interval fall on the Columbus Day weekend, when more people flew than the previous weeks suggested. Clairic forecasts from the patterns in the series but doesn't account for events the series doesn't show, like holidays. Thinking fast and slow These models are designed to fit alongside your existing agentic workflows. An extraction model predicts values, a decision model decides what to do with these values, and an LLM takes action with them. It is a perfect marriage between System One and System Two models. It bridges the existing gap, where you either have to manually extract data for LLMs, or have an LLM parse through messy data (which is costly, time-consuming, and can lead to hallucinations). With System One extraction models, you can work with real-world data with more speed, efficiency, and precision. Here's an example of the damaged-product claim from earlier, illustrating how all the models can work together. We built this into a live demo you can try here. // 1. Clairic turns the email into values const facts = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", { state: email, fields: { customer_name: { type: "text", instructions: "Customer's first name" }, order_id: { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" }, amount_paid: { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" }, days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true, instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" }, damage: { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" }, repair_cost: { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 10, max: 5000, scale: "log", step: 1, instructions: "Cost to repair the damage described" }, }, })).answers; const { customer_name, order_id, amount_paid, days_since_delivery, damage, repair_cost } = facts; // 2. Clef decides from Clairic's values and the policy, not from the raw email const options = { refund: "Full refund of the amount paid", repair: "Free repair, with a prepaid shipping label", }; const { choice } = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clef", { state: `Damage claim for order ${order_id.value}. Paid: $${amount_paid.value.toFixed(2)}. Delivered ${days_since_delivery.value} days ago. Damage reported: ${damage.value.join(", ")}. Estimated repair cost: $${repair_cost.median} (80% range $${repair_cost.p10}-$${repair_cost.p90}). Policy: refunds within 30 days of delivery. Prefer repair when it costs less than 60% of the price and the damage doesn't stop the product from working.`, questions: { resolution: { type: "choice", instructions: "What should we offer?", criteria: options }, }, })).answers.resolution; // 3. An LLM writes the reply, from the decision and the facts it needs const { response } = await env.AI.run("@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3", { messages: [{ role: "user", content: `Write a short, warm reply to ${customer_name.value}. Use only these facts: order ${order_id.value}; ` + `damage: ${damage.value.join(", ")}; what happens next: ${options[choice]}. Under 60 words.`, }], }); Each step gets cleaner input than the one before. Clef decides from a five-line summary of typed values instead of a free-form email, which can also be susceptible to prompt injection. The LLM never sees the email, only the decision and the predictions it needs, so there are fewer numbers for it to misuse. Every step is typed and auditable, and only one step generates text. In the all-LLM version of this pipeline, all three steps are generative calls, and every value in the reply has to be checked by hand. We ran this pipeline against an all-LLM version with GLM-5.3 writing the reply in both. In the all-LLM version, GLM-5.3 also does the extraction and the decision, from the same email, policy and prompts: Clairic → Clef → GLM-5.3 GLM-5.3 for every step Latency, end to end 19.3 s 61.7 s 1. Extract Clairic: 0.46 s GLM-5.3: 16.1 s 2. Decide Clef: 0.22 s GLM-5.3: 21.9 s 3. Reply GLM-5.3: 18.6 s GLM-5.3: 16.4 s Input tokens 701 ($184 per million claims) 390 ($546 per million claims) Output tokens 1,329 ($5,848 per million claims) 2,544 ($11,194 per million claims) Cost per million claims $6,032 $11,740 The cascade finished in 19.3 seconds against 61.7 seconds: 69% less time, or about 3.2 times faster. Clairic and Clef handled extraction and the decision in under a second combined, where GLM-5.3 took 38 seconds for the same two steps. It also costs 49% less to use the cascaded pipeline vs the all-LLM pipeline. With GLM, both pipelines got the facts and the decision right in every run, but Clairic's repair estimate was identical each time, while GLM-5.3's changed on every run ($250, $250 and $220, with different ranges each time). Notably, under the all-LLM pipeline both Gemma 4 and Qwen failed at this task, as they were unable to deduce values like repair_cost from the inputs, showing how LLMs are not great at data extraction tasks. Preview release Today, we're releasing a hosted endpoint for Clairic on Workers AI. We intend to release the model with open weights soon. We wanted to take the time first to introduce the concept of a System One extraction model, so you can start thinking about how this class of model would fit into appropriate workflows. The current endpoint is an early checkpoint and we expect it to get better. Here are our early impressions: Reading is strong, but multi-step arithmetic isn't yet. One- and two-step calculations (totals, differences, conversions, date arithmetic) seem reliable. Longer chains of dependent steps are hard for any one-pass model without a scratchpad. The same goes for aggregating across many rows of a table. At least for now, have Clairic predict the value and let code do the math. Estimates need evidence. Clairic estimates best from comparables, history, or descriptive text in the input. Asking it for a value it has no evidence for may be limited in specificity. Calibration is measured, not guaranteed. Intervals are trained to be calibrated and are on most held-out sets, but they can run narrow on unfamiliar data. Forecasting is basic. The model is not designed to accurately replace or predict time-series models that are trained on specific data. You should use it where appropriate, such as non-critical, general pattern matching, not detailed long-horizon forecasting. Use confidence. The architecture makes every answer well formed, not necessarily correct. Use confidence, p_null and the intervals to decide what to automate (in an appropriate workflow context) and what to send off for additional review. We'll keep working on the arithmetic, estimation and forecasting sides of the model with each checkpoint. After some more work, we plan to release the model open-weights for everyone to play around with as well. Try it out Clairic is available as a preview on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. Call it from a Worker with env.AI.run(), or from anywhere with the REST API. We have full model docs here, as well as a new docs explainer on how the extraction model API looks. P.S. Since you liked the etymology of the name Clef, here’s how we landed on the name Clairic. We started with a desire to keep the name of the model thematically and sonically similar to Clef. Clair came to mind, sharing the same “cl” sound, as well as roots in music (“Clair de Lune”). More importantly, we wanted the name to be descriptive to the nature of the model. The Clairic model should be able to help you with clerical tasks like extracting data clearly from a corpus of inputs and upholding accuracy in tasks like bookkeeping. The prediction aspect of the model leans into the “Clair” root — allowing you to estimate and predict future values, similar to clairvoyance. Lastly, we like the idea of having this be [Cl]oudflare’s [AI R]egression model. Thus, Clairic was born into the world. We hope you enjoy it.

items.title: Announcing Privacy Badger for Safari on macOS
items.author: Lena Cohen
items.content: Exciting news for Safari users: Privacy Badger is now available on Safari for macOS! You’ll need Safari version 26.5 or higher to use it. Whether you want to protect yourself from data brokers or just don’t want Big Tech profiting off your browsing data, Privacy Badger is here to help. More than 4 million people already use EFF’s free tracker-blocking extension to take a stand against online surveillance. Safari users can now join them and EFF in the fight for a better web. Install Privacy Badger Support the Fight Against Online Tracking Safari support has been one of Privacy Badger’s most requested features for years. Thanks to recent improvements in Safari's extension support, we’ve finally made it happen for Safari version 26.5 and higher. Privacy Badger is now available on all major desktop browsers. And before you ask, yes, we will look into supporting Safari for iOS once we've ironed out any issues on macOS. Why Install Privacy Badger on Safari? Most websites contain invisible tracking code that lets companies collect, share, and profit from your personal data. Some of those companies are data brokers that sell your information to anyone willing to pay. Creepy ads are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the harms of online tracking: Once your information enters the data broker ecosystem, it’s nearly impossible to know who buys it or what they’re doing with it. Privacy Badger blocks online trackers to prevent your browsing data from being used against you. Privacy Badger goes beyond Safari’s built-in privacy features to provide additional protection against online tracking. In its default browsing mode, Safari limits the information that trackers can access but still allows them to load. Privacy Badger blocks trackers from loading in the first place, preventing them from tracking you using techniques that bypass Safari’s protections. Privacy Badger works well by itself, and will continue to enhance your privacy when installed along side an ad blocker or with Safari’s Advanced settings to block trackers in all windows. Since Privacy Badger automatically learns to block trackers, Privacy Badger will block trackers that other tools don’t know about or choose not to block. For example, Privacy Badger blocks tracking from widgets like embedded tweets, comments sections, and video players. These widgets can share your data even if you never click on them. Privacy Badger prevents these trackers from loading and replaces them with click-to-activate placeholders. Beyond tracker blocking, Privacy Badger automatically sends the Global Privacy Control (GPC) signal to tell websites not to sell or share your personal information. The GPC signal is already legally binding in a growing number of states, including California, Colorado, New Jersey, and Connecticut. All these features (and more) work together to help keep your browsing activity private on Safari. Try It Out and Spread the Word If you use Safari on macOS, give Privacy Badger a try. You’ll install Privacy Badger through the App Store on your macOS device. Installing extensions is a little more complicated on Safari than other browsers, so follow Apple’s directions here if you’re having trouble. This is our first release of Privacy Badger for Safari, and we will keep improving it based on your feedback. If you run into any problems, let us know by emailing extension-devs@eff.org, or by opening an issue on GitHub. And if blocking harmful trackers causes issues on a website you visit, you can disable Privacy Badger for that specific site while keeping it enabled and protecting you everywhere else. You can also let us know about broken sites by using the “Report broken site” button found next to the “Disable for this site” button in Privacy Badger’s popup window. When you use Privacy Badger, you join EFF and millions of other users in the fight for a better web. Help spread the word by telling your friends and family who use Safari that they can use Privacy Badger too! Install Privacy Badger Support the Fight Against Online Tracking

items.title: ReactOS reaches major milestone with NTFS install support
items.author: Nick Indge
items.content: Open source Windows alternative ReactOS has reached a major milestone: The operating system can now be installed directly onto an NT Files System drive partition. As reported by Phoronix, the move to NTFS clears a long-standing hurdle for the project and brings it one step closer to finally reaching beta. Prior to this latest announcement, ReactOS required users to keep a FAT32 partition for installations. A proprietary Microsoft-developed filesystem, NTFS can trace its roots back through the Windows NT family lineage starting in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1. The variant introduced with Windows XP in 2001 remains the standard used by most Windows systems today. With ReactOS's stated goal of reaching binary compatibility with Windows Server 2003, being confined to FAT32 partitions was a practical barrier to clear on the way to reproducing the Windows environment. However, users looking to hop off the Windows train shouldn't be grabbing their bags just yet. ReactOS wrote that the new driver still "lacks caching (which causes inferior performance), journaling and security support." So while the new driver is here, even the most intrepid of OS tinkerers should tread carefully. The ReactOS team warned in its announcement on X that there are still "potentially undiscovered bugs." Read full article Comments

items.title: How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code
items.author: Kayla Cinnamon
items.content: The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it. But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app… and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code? You don’t. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing. In this tutorial, you’ll learn how to: Open a Copilot app session in VS Code. Review the agent’s changes line by line. Continue the same conversation from your editor. Modify and test the code locally. Push your updates to the pull request associated with the session. Prerequisites Before you begin, make sure you have: The GitHub Copilot app installed and signed in. Visual Studio Code installed and connected to the same GitHub account. A Copilot app session with code changes you want to review or continue. Permission to work in and push changes to the session’s repository. This tutorial assumes you are already comfortable navigating VS Code, running commands in its integrated terminal, and working with Git branches and pull requests. 1. Start with a session in the Copilot app Open the session you want to continue. Before handing it off, take a moment to review the task and the work Copilot completed. A session contains more than a collection of modified files. It also records the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes. That context is important when you want to understand why Copilot chose a particular implementation or ask it to revise part of the work. You do not need to summarize that history or copy it into a new chat before moving to VS Code. 2. Open the session in VS Code From the session, select Open in VS Code. If the app presents more than one supported editor or VS Code installation, choose the one you want to use. VS Code opens the project using the worktree associated with the session. It also displays the existing session in the Copilot sidebar. That gives you three connected pieces of the original work: The session context: The task, plan, and conversation remain available. The diff: The files and lines changed by the agent are ready for review. The worktree: VS Code opens the same isolated working tree the session used. You are continuing the existing session, not reconstructing it in a new editor window. 3. Review the agent’s changes Before editing, inspect the diff in VS Code. Open the Source Control view to see the changed files, then select a file to review its changes line by line. Review the implementation as you would any other proposed change. In particular, check that: The code solves the requested problem. The implementation follows the repository’s conventions. Error states and edge cases are handled appropriately. Tests cover the behavior that changed. No unrelated files or behaviors were modified. The preserved conversation can help explain how Copilot arrived at the implementation. If something is unclear, continue prompting Copilot in the sidebar. For example: Explain why you changed this function instead of adding a new helper. Identify any behavior this could affect. You can also ask Copilot to make another change. Because the session and worktree remain connected, you do not have to describe the task from the beginning. 4. Make a hands-on edit Once you understand the proposed changes, edit any file directly in VS Code. This is useful for adjustments that are faster or easier to make by hand, such as: Refining a label or error message. Renaming a variable for clarity. Adjusting layout or styling. Adding a missing test case. Applying a repository-specific convention. You are editing the session’s existing worktree, so your manual changes build directly on the agent’s work. You do not need to copy files between directories or manually re-create the branch. 5. Run and verify the project locally Use the VS Code integrated terminal to run the project’s normal validation workflow. The exact commands depend on the repository, but some web app examples may include: npm install npm test npm run lint npm run dev Treat agent-generated changes the same way you would treat code written by a person: run the relevant tests, inspect failures, and verify the behavior yourself. If the development server prints a localhost URL, open it to test the change in a browser. When supported by your VS Code setup, you can open the URL in VS Code’s integrated browser and inspect the result without leaving the editor. For a user-interface change, verify both the requested behavior and nearby states. For example, check the modified component at different viewport sizes and confirm that loading, empty, and error states still work. 6. Continue with Copilot or keep editing yourself At any point, you can choose the interaction that best fits the next step: Prompt Copilot when the change requires repository-wide analysis or repetitive edits. Edit directly when you know the exact change you want. Use both approaches iteratively as you test and refine the implementation. For example, after making a manual UI adjustment, you might ask Copilot: Add a test for the updated label and run the relevant test file. Do not modify unrelated components. Because you are still in the original session, Copilot retains the context needed to interpret “the updated label.” 7. Commit and push the finished changes When the implementation is ready, review the final diff one more time. Then commit and push the changes using the Source Control view or the integrated terminal: git status git add git commit -m "Refine session changes" git push Use your repository’s normal branch, commit, review, and approval practices. Because VS Code opened the worktree and branch associated with the session, pushing the branch updates the pull request already tracking that work. There is no need to copy the finished files into another checkout or reconnect the work to the pull request manually. A continuous workflow from agent to editor Opening a Copilot app session in VS Code gives you a clean division of labor without splitting the work itself. Copilot can take on a larger or repetitive implementation, while you can move into the editor for detailed review, targeted changes, local testing, and final polish. The session, diff, and worktree move with you. Start by directing the work in the Copilot app, switch to VS Code whenever you want hands-on control, and push the finished result through the same pull request workflow. Ready to try it? Download the GitHub Copilot app, start a session, and open it in VS Code when you are ready to continue coding. The post How to continue a GitHub Copilot app session in VS Code appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
