items.title: Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
items.author: Ryan Skidmore
items.content: When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April, an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave. Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before. About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in. How a review doubled in cost The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data. The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though. At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models. Our internal standards reviewer, Codex, ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself. The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost. What else has changed since our last post? One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable. We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out! So, where were the tokens going? Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%, cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again. That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both. It’s worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cache works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from what’s been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so they’re a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it. That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls. Sharing a cached prefix between every repository Beginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider. The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits. The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. The shared part was never stored on its own, so a review in one repository could never reuse what a reviewer ran in another repository had written. On September 16, we added a marker to the end of every agent prompt and a plugin hook that split the block in two at that marker. The first half now ended on bytes that every job shares, and got its own breakpoint. To keep it that way we had to remove anything repository-specific from in front of it, so the list of available skills is disabled and tool descriptions can't change between jobs. The same day we also moved our internal standards (Codex) reviewer's reference index (a table of internal standards, a skill file and a list of reference files) into its prompt. Until then every session had spent its first three turns reading those files with tool calls. Its LLM calls per run decreased from 15.9 to 9.6, and its cost per run dropped from $1.12 to $0.72. Together these took the cost per review from $2.47 down to $2.02, and the drop was noticeable as soon as we kicked off the release. Fewer calls, fewer dollars The next set of changes went out on September 21 and 23. None of them were particularly impressive by themselves, but together they took about $0.20 off every review. Change What was happening Effect of change Removing tools that reviewers couldn't use Sub-reviewers could see the tool that posts the final review comment. In 57% to 76% of sessions they tried to call it, were rejected by a check on the server, and spent another call recovering. One wasted call gone, and about 2.9k fewer tokens of tool definitions in every sub-reviewer request Reading files in parallel In 64% of the code quality reviewer's turns, the model made exactly one tool call, usually to read a single file. Reviewers read the shared context and all of their patches in their first response, up to 150 KB Skipping reviewers on re-reviews About two-thirds of our jobs are a second or later review of the same merge request, and often three of the reviewers have nothing new to look at. On full-tier re-reviews, AGENTS.md reviews are skipped 56% of the time, performance reviews skipped 23% and documentation reviews skipped 13%. Stopping after the review is posted OpenCode passed the result back to the model for one more turn, which read the entire conversation again to write a summary nobody saw. About $0.07 saved per job Treating a slow reviewer differently from a broken provider A reviewer that hit its time limit was treated like a provider failure and started again with the same time limit. Together with longer time limits and lower effort, security reviewer timeouts went from 1.8% of runs to almost none Canceling canceled jobs GitLab's Kubernetes executor doesn't send a signal to a job's script when the job is cancelled. In a sample of 446 cancelled jobs, 358 kept running until the review was finished. Jobs check their own status every 15 seconds and stop if cancelled The most involved change was sharing one prefix between three reviewers. The code quality, security, and performance reviewers now send identical first requests with the same tools, a shared rules file, then the merge request with every patch included. Each reviewer's own instructions follow after that, and we make sure that one of them writes the cache and the other two read from it. A cache entry can't be read until the response that wrote it has started streaming, and the three reviewers start at the same time. So the second and third wait for the first one's response to begin, for up to 20 seconds, before sending their own first request. It slows them down slightly and saves about nine cents per reviewer. Changing models and effort The next chart shows the same line from the start of September, with each change marked. When we split the period at every release and every configuration change, the code changes turn out to be the smaller part of the saving. Code changes account for $0.65 of the $1.67, and model and effort changes for $1.06. Each step compares the weekday hours before a change with the hours after it, so this isn't a statistically sound controlled experiment. The coordinator had been running three model and effort combinations since August. On the same model, full-tier jobs on medium effort finished 20% sooner, so we dropped the other two. In a later randomized split, Opus 5.5 at medium showed no measurable change in review outcomes or critical findings compared with Opus 5, so we switched. Opus 5.5 at high effort cost more than Opus 5.5 at medium while not producing a meaningful increase in findings. Opus 5.5 is cheaper per token than Opus 5, but price is only responsible for about $0.20 of the drop. The rest comes from sending and generating fewer tokens. Since the start of September cache reads per review are down 82%, cache writes down 54%, and output down 67%. The most recent change was a new model. On October 3, we split every Sonnet reviewer 50/50 between Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5. After two and a half days, Sonnet 5.5 was 62% cheaper per run for code quality, 58% for performance and 47% for security. The two models cost the same per token, so all of that comes from using fewer tokens. On full-tier reviews, the 5.5 reviewers posted about as many critical and warning findings as the Sonnet 5 ones, so on October 5 we moved all of them to 5.5. On Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, the code quality reviewer makes 1.7 LLM calls per run instead of 6.2, and more than half of its runs finish in a single call, which means they don't open any other file in the repository. At high effort it makes 3.4 calls per run. We were concerned that this made reviews shallower, which we cover in the quality section below. To see whether more effort brings findings back on the larger tiers, the code quality reviewer has been split 50/50 between medium and high effort on 5.5 since October 5. After one day, high effort costs 61% more per run and posts 58% more critical and warning findings. That's about two cents per review, and the quality section below shows those extra findings are worth having, so we're moving code quality to high effort. The cost figures in this post assume that. Latency We weren't aiming to make reviews faster, but fewer calls also means less waiting, which means faster reviews and happier engineers. The slowest reviews improved the most. In the four weeks before September 14, 37.9% of reviews took longer than five minutes and now just 0.7% do. The 99th percentile today is faster than three quarters of reviews were in April. Every tier got faster along the way with the median full-tier review going from 5m 16s to 1m 54s, lite from 2m 58s to 1m 14s, and trivial from 77 seconds to 30. By August, the median review was 14% slower than what we reported in April and the 99th percentile 48% slower, so a good part of this work just got us back to where we had been. Review quality A cheaper review isn't worth much if it also finds fewer problems, and the first chart here looks like that's what happened. With code quality on Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, it posts 40% fewer critical and warning findings than it did in late August. Security and performance, which stay at medium effort, post 56% and 71% fewer. A fall in severe findings doesn't tell you on its own whether real problems are being missed or noise is being cut, so we looked at it from two directions. First, we checked whether authors act on what the reviewer flags. For samples of critical and warning findings, we compared the commit that was reviewed with the author's next push, and counted a finding as acted on if the lines it pointed at had changed. Lines 30 to 40 away from each finding changed about 15% of the time in every period, which gives a baseline for edits that happen by coincidence. Before the changes, authors acted on 34% of the code quality reviewer's serious findings. Now it's 59%. The reviewer flags fewer things, but those it flags are much more likely to lead to a change, so the number of findings that led to a change per 1,000 reviews is about the same. We now saw 132 against 145 before, which is within the margin of error. Across all four reviewers, serious findings that led to a change went from 229 to 321 per 1,000 reviews. Second, we had two models from different providers judge a blinded sample of 657 findings from the three Sonnet reviewers, with the diff each one referred to and without knowing which period it came from. Disagreements went to a third model. Each finding was labelled important, minor, duplicate, wrong, or unverifiable, and its severity was marked as fair, too high, or too low. Most of what disappeared was minor findings, plus some duplicates and findings the judges couldn't verify from the diff. Important findings per review went from 0.28 before to 0.30 now, and the intervals overlap. The bigger change was in severity. Before, the judges rated 0.46 critical or warning findings per review as more severe than they deserved. Now that's 0.14, a 70% drop and the clearest result in the research. Much of the drop in critical findings is the reviewer no longer calling minor things critical. So the answer depends on the reviewer. For code quality at high effort, what disappeared was mostly noise and inflated severity, and it still finds about as many real problems as before. Medium effort did lose real findings. In the randomized split, code quality at medium led to roughly a quarter as many acted-on findings as at high, which is why we're moving it to high. Performance also lost real findings: the judges found about 64% fewer important performance issues per review, which in practice is about one fewer important finding every 24 full-tier reviews. Security fell by about a quarter, though that isn't statistically significant. Both are still at medium effort, and testing them at high is next. Neither method is perfect. An author changing the flagged lines shows they did something, not that the finding was right. The judges are models too, and there are only 35 to 66 findings in each group. The "now" window is also only a day long. Even so, the two methods agree with each other, and neither suggests that code quality is finding fewer real problems. Reliability has held up as well. Reviews that end without a verdict went from 0.79% to 0.27%, and security reviewer retries from 3.5% to 0.04%. Where this leaves us An average review now costs $0.77 instead of $2.43, and the median one finishes in 1m 32s instead of 4m 9s. The biggest single saving came from checking what actually reached the provider on each session’s first request, and finding a way to order those messages in a way that was as consistent as possible across commits, merge requests and repositories. The remaining cost savings came from relentlessly experimenting with different models and effort mixes, while making sure we put any preconceived bias for particular models aside. Lower cost reviews didn’t automatically mean worse quality, but it didn’t automatically mean fine either. Code quality at high effort finds about as many real problems as before, with much less noise and far fewer inflated severities. Performance lost real findings at medium effort, and security may have, too, so testing both at high effort is next. If you run agents at any kind of volume, the two things we’d check first are whether each session’s first request actually reads from the cache, and whether your reviewers still find real problems at the effort level you’re paying for. If you’re at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco, I’m talking about how we built the reviewer instead of buying one in my session, It’s time to build, not buy, on Tuesday, October 20 at 12:30 PM PDT. I’ll also be in the Speaker Connection Lounge from 1:10 PM if you want to ask about any of the numbers in this post.

items.title: Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in "proof point" test
items.author: Jeremy Hsu
items.content: The world’s first demonstration of a subsea geothermal power plant has taken place near an active underwater volcano almost a mile below the ocean surface. It generated less than 10 seconds of net-positive electricity but showed the technical feasibility of tapping another form of renewable energy underwater. The three-week test deployment of the 3-ton prototype power plant took place at the Axial Seamount in the northeast Pacific Ocean in September. Endurance Energy, the Seattle-based startup behind the effort, aims to eventually commercialize subsea geothermal power for Pacific island nations and other customers looking for alternatives to importing expensive fossil fuels. “The deep ocean gives us unlimited cold seawater for cooling, and its weight keeps the system and the well pressurized, so our plants can be compact,” said Andrew Redd, founder and CEO of Endurance Energy, in an email to Ars. Read full article Comments

items.title: New paper: Emerging trends in AI agent evaluation
items.author: Sayash Kapoor
items.content: By Felix Chen, Stephan Rabanser, Sayash Kapoor, and Arvind Narayanan. See the full author list and affiliations here. There are growing calls for independent and embedded AI evaluation, especially of AI agents. But much remains unclear: what constitutes a “good” evaluation, what needs to be evaluated in the first place, and how best to coordinate and support the influx of people entering the burgeoning evaluation ecosystem. Our group at Princeton has been working to improve the state of AI agent evaluation for about three years. We teamed up with people who’ve done foundational work on evaluation at Stanford, the UK AI Security Institute, and Brookings. Our paper is titled Emerging Trends in AI Agent Evaluation. We synthesized the trends we see across three dimensions—the science and methods, the research agenda, and the evaluation ecosystem—with the goal to help those who are upskilling for this new paradigm. We also aim to equip evaluators, funders, and the public with a set of questions to ask, and provide actionable recommendations. Thirty-three emerging trends in AI agent evaluation. (Figure from the paper.) Challenges for agents, new and old AI developers have long made claims about the real-world performance of their systems based on benchmark scores. It is harder now to assess whether the evidence gathered supports claims made about agents. The evaluator must scrutinize the entire trajectory, not just the final outcome. It is important, for example, to know if agents took shortcuts, particularly since they have access to tools and environments. And when agents perform better or worse, it is harder to attribute these changes to different components of the agent. Addressing these concerns requires significant engineering effort, and the work is getting increasingly expensive—for example, several agents on the ExploitBench benchmark cost tens of thousands of dollars in credits to evaluate. These numbers also don’t factor in the significant engineering effort needed to set up and maintain the evaluation infrastructure itself. Agent evaluation is much more complex than model evaluation. (Figure from the paper.) Faced with the massive volume of traces that agents generate, evaluators are also struggling to inspect and monitor these agents at scale. The tools evaluators rely on today to do this work are not foolproof—and themselves require evaluation. To investigate the recent OpenAI-HuggingFace incident after the fact, evaluators relied upon other agents to look for and identify instances of harmful action, an approach they acknowledged carried its own limitations and biases. Because agents are deployed in dynamic settings (and increasingly together with other agents), it is harder to design good metrics to capture the underlying concepts of interest, and create valid conditions to implement them. Addressing these challenges will require better tools, more rigorous benchmarks, and experimentation with different approaches and formats, such as through open-world evaluations and growing observational data on real-world usage. The scope of evaluation needs is growing Evidence about agents is needed to understand their effects at different layers, but does not always translate across layers. (Figure from the paper.) Crucially, the results of evaluation at one level of scope are not guaranteed to translate to another. An agent might demonstrate capability in the lab, but face limits when placed in a specific use case. Consider METR’s randomized controlled trial which found that, despite expectations, usage of agent tools toward software development actually increased overall completion time on the tasks at hand. Agents may be able to perform certain tasks, but how that capability translates for humans in the real world requires evaluation in context. An expanded research agenda is therefore needed to understand agents at each level: their capabilities, their interactions with humans, and their impact on institutions and incentive structures. This work requires both technical and sociotechnical evaluation to study not just the agent itself but the agent(s) in context. Across these different layers, evaluators have a choice in framing the questions they ask and the findings they generate. Can an agent automate a task or process? Or, can an agent augment the work of a human? These are two complementary lenses. If evaluation largely focuses on how agents automate certain tasks, we will better understand where and how human work can be replaced. But it won’t tell us how humans can better collaborate using agents, or how agents can improve human work. Who gets to evaluate and how? This expanded research agenda will require an expanded set of evaluators from a mix of disciplines. It will also require that evaluators have the freedom to choose which questions to pursue and how. When evaluators with different approaches agree, we might gain greater confidence in those results. And when they conflict, evaluators can identify vague definitions and limitations to their findings. Who gets to participate, and with what independence, will shape the questions evaluators ask and the methods they use. Meaningful independence is influenced by several factors. As the costs of frontier evaluation keep increasing, the ability of independent evaluators to participate will be increasingly determined by their access to increased funding. Whether independent evaluators have sufficient access to models also impacts their ability to measure and assess the true frontier. Questions of access now also extend to Chain of Thought traces for agents, since frontier labs now release summarized versions instead of raw traces. Alongside these challenges, evaluators also need to navigate whether they can conduct work without fear of retaliation, and how they can transparently share their findings. Where do we go from here? There is a clear window now to bring in new participants, methods, and ideas for agent evaluations, and to meet the pressing need for rigorous evidence in a fast-moving space. We hope this paper gives readers an emerging sense of the field’s direction. There are many steps that stakeholders in the AI evaluation community can take to advance the science and practice of AI evaluation. For prospective evaluators, there is a need to determine what roles or questions within this ecosystem best fit their expertise, and examine which dimensions of independence are required for that work. In particular, we encourage participation from disciplines not yet engaged in AI evaluation; there are many open challenges that can benefit from their perspectives. For current evaluators, there is an opportunity to examine their own methodological assumptions and embrace perspectives from other disciplines; this field of agent evaluation is inherently interdisciplinary, and will necessarily involve some rediscovery and reinvention of existing ideas and insights. For field-builders—funders, coalitions, and conference organizers—agent evaluation demands its own field of practice, one with higher standards for validity and rigor. Raising this bar can happen by coalescing best practices and fostering conversation and engagement between different disciplinary perspectives. For leaderboard aggregators, who are central to this emerging ecosystem by shaping which dimensions of evaluation receive attention and in what manner, there is a prime opportunity to incorporate best practices around reporting for downstream adoption, and to help the public understand the rising costs of evaluation. For deployers and industry evaluators, there is a critical gap for real-world settings to inform evaluation work. By contributing on-the-ground insights and engaging with work in the lab, they can strengthen the discourse in this fast-moving space. For labs, there is an opportunity to build bridges with independent evaluators and examine the community’s best practices. Successful embedded evaluators will require public legitimacy through independence, transparency, and methodological rigor. For policymakers, there is a need to develop a clear sense of the current ecosystem and what good evaluations should look like. And for public sector deployments, evaluation needs to be an integrated and continuous part of the process from day one. AISIs can play a key role by pioneering new models for collaboration and inviting new stakeholders into their public input mechanisms within the current ecosystem. Read the paper here.
